OPINION AFFIRMING IN PART, 
VACATING IN PART, AND REMANDING 

** ** ** ** ** 

BEFORE: CALDWELL, L. JONES, AND TAYLOR, JUDGES. 
JONES, L., JUDGE: Audrey Lynn Arcelli and Ms. Audrey’s Crafting Emporium, 
LLC (collectively Appellants) appeal the September 30, 2024 order of the 
Jefferson Circuit Court granting summary judgment in favor of Ghasem Properties, 
Inc. (GPI).1 We affirm the circuit court’s grant of summary judgment except as to 

1 Appellants’ notice of appeal states that they are appealing from: 

the Summary Judgment entered by [the circuit court] September 
30, 2024[,] and from the [circuit court’s] Order entered [] 

 -2- 
its award of 8% prejudgment interest and future rents for damages accruing after 
entry of the judgment on September 30, 2024. 
I. BACKGROUND 
 On February 8, 2023, Ms. Audrey’s Crafting Emporium, LLC entered 
into a commercial lease with GPI to rent certain retail space for sixty-two months. 
On that same date, Audrey Arcelli (Arcelli) executed a guaranty agreement, 
wherein Arcelli would be guarantor for the lease up to the amount of $155,124.60. 
Under the lease, Appellants were to pay $2,585.41 monthly for rent and 
community area maintenance beginning the third month of the lease term. 
 On April 8, 2024, GPI filed suit in Jefferson Circuit Court, alleging 
Appellants defaulted under the lease by failing to pay the January 2024 rental 
obligation or any rental payments going forward. GPI alleged it provided notice 
by mail on January 6, 2024, that Appellants had not paid their January 2024 rent 
obligation, and that the lease would be terminated in seven days if rent and late 

December 11, 2024[,] denying [Appellants’] motion to alter, 
amend or vacate the aforementioned Summary Judgment under 
provisions of CR (Kentucky Rules of Civil Procedure) 59, and 
granting [GPI’s] motion for a Supplemental Judgment for 
attorney’s fees and costs. 

Trial Record (TR) at 264. However, it is well settled that a party may not appeal denial of a 
motion under Kentucky Rules of Civil Procedure (CR) 59.05, as the appeal is from the 
underlying judgment rather than the CR 59.05 motion itself. Ford v. Ford, 578 S.W.3d 356, 366 
(Ky. App. 2019). We note that the circuit court denied Appellants’ CR 59.05 motion and granted 
supplemental judgment to GPI in the same order; however, Appellants make no arguments in 
this appeal about the merits of supplemental judgment. 

 -3- 
fees were not paid. GPI alleged that, due to default, it was entitled to lost lease 
payments, advertising costs, and accruing late fees. GPI also claimed it was 
entitled to statutory prejudgment interest from January 1, 2024, to the date of 
judgment; post judgment interest; attorney fees; and court costs.2 Attached to 
GPI’s complaint was a copy of the lease agreement, the guaranty agreement 
executed by Arcelli, and the January 6, 2024 notice. 
 On April 19, 2024, Appellants filed an answer. In that answer, 
Appellants admitted to signing the lease, defaulting under the lease, and not paying 
rents under the lease for January 2024 and forward. As to the other documents 
attached to the complaint, Appellants responded those exhibits “speak for 
[themselves].”3 Additionally, Appellants denied responsibility for damages. 
 On August 31, 2024, GPI filed a motion for summary judgment, 
asserting there were no genuine issues of material fact and it was entitled to 
judgment as a matter of law. Attached to that motion was an affidavit executed by 
Reza Ghasem (Ghasem), president of GPI. In that affidavit, Ghasem averred: (1) 
Ms. Audrey’s Crafting Emporium entered into a lease agreement with GPI on

Jefferson District Court, though that action was dismissed in April 2024 after Appellants vacated 
the property. TR at 4. While Appellants asserted in their Answer that “the record in the []

Rental payments were to begin on the third month of the lease in the amount of 
$2,089.58 and “additional monthly common area maintenance . . . payments of 
$495.83 for a combined monthly total of $2,585.41 plus monthly trash payments, 
and such other expenses as more fully set forth therein [the lease agreement]”;4 (3) 
Appellants defaulted on the lease by failing to pay rent for January 2024; (4) GPI 
gave notice of failure to pay the rent for January 2024, demanded payment of rent 
and late fees, and provided notice that failure to pay would result in termination of 
the lease and legal recourse; (5) Following the notice, Appellants never remitted 
payment; (6) GPI sought a forcible detainer, but Appellants vacated the property; 
(7) Appellants refused any further demands for additional payment under the lease; 
(8) GPI entered into a commercial listing contract to locate a new tenant to 
mitigate damages with no success; (9) Between January 2024 and April 2028,5 
Appellants “would have paid a principal total of $131,855.91”;6 and (10) 
Appellants owe GPI that principal amount, “statutory prejudgment interest” from 
the date of default to judgment, post judgment interest “at the statutory rate,” 

4 TR at 74. 

5 The remaining lease term. 

6 TR at 77. 

 -5- 
accrued interest, late fees, attorney fees, court costs, and expenses.7 Attached to 
Ghasem’s affidavit was a copy of the lease agreement, a copy of the guaranty 
agreement, a copy of the January 6, 2024 notice, and a copy of a commercial 
listing contract for the leased property. 
 Appellants never responded to GPI’s motion for summary judgment. 
There was no hearing on the summary judgment motion; instead, on September 26, 
2024, GPI filed an AOC8 280 Form Notice of Submission of Civil Matter for Final 
Adjudication, noting the summary judgment motion was ripe for adjudication. On 
September 30, 2024, the circuit court granted GPI’s motion for summary judgment 
utilizing an order tendered by GPI. Under that judgment, GPI was awarded 
“$131,855.91, with prejudgment interest at the rate of 8% per annum from January 
1, 2024[,] until the date of this judgment, thence post judgment interest at the rate 
of 6% per annum until paid in full, plus reasonable attorney fees, court costs and 
expenses.”9 
 On October 10, 2024, Appellants filed a motion to vacate the circuit 
court’s judgment pursuant to CR 59.05 (59.05 Motion). In their 59.05 Motion, 
Appellants made two arguments: (1) GPI failed to surmount its “initial burden” to 

7 TR at 77. 

8 Administrative Office of the Courts. 

9 TR at 130-31. 

 -6- 
establish there were no genuine issues of material fact, and, thus, the summary 
judgment motion should have been denied without requiring Appellants to offer 
any supporting evidence; and (2) the circuit court might have erred by granting 
summary judgment based on unsworn statements by GPI’s counsel.10 
 In response, GPI stated: (1) All claims in its motion for summary 
judgment were supported by Ghasem’s affidavit; (2) Appellants’ argument that the 
circuit court based its ruling on unsworn statements of counsel was vague and 
speculative; and (3) Even if the circuit court erred, Appellants have failed to show 
the error was manifest under CR 59.05.11 
 Appellants filed a reply, further asserting that Ghasem’s affidavit was 
flawed as Ghasem claimed his knowledge was drawn from “certain business 
records” without specifically stating the records attached to his affidavit were the 
only business records to which his affidavit referred.12 Furthermore, Appellants 
claimed Ghasem’s affidavit did not clearly set out the basis for the $131,855.91 
claimed as damages. For the first time, Appellants also argued that nothing in the 

10 TR at 137-40. 

11 TR at 141-46. 

12 TR at 247. 

 -7- 
lease agreement entitled GPI to future rental payments for the life of the lease as 
liquidated damages, or 8% prejudgment interest.13 
 On December 11, 2024, the circuit court entered an order denying 
Appellants CR 59.05 Motion.14 In that order, the trial court noted Appellants never 
responded to the summary judgment motion and their arguments “could and should 
have been made prior to the entry of the judgment.”15 
 On appeal, Appellants continue to argue that Ghasem’s affidavit failed 
to show there was no genuine issue of material fact. In particular, Appellants 
assert Ghasem’s affidavit does not state that his personal knowledge and the 
attached exhibits are the sole foundation from which he claims damages of 
$131,855.91. Appellants further argue the lease agreement does not contain a 
liquidated damages clause or other provision which would entitle GPI to lost rental 
payments for the remainder of the lease period. Finally, Appellants assert that 
nowhere in Ghasem’s affidavit or lease agreement was there a claim for 8% 
prejudgment interest. 

13 TR at 251-52. 

14 In that same order, the circuit court entered a supplemental judgment, awarding GPI $8,299.30 
in attorney fees and court costs. On October 31, 2024, GPI had filed a motion requesting 
attorney fees and costs. Appellants filed no objection to GPI’s requests for attorney fees and 
costs, nor did Appellants appear at the hearing on that motion. 

15 TR at 258. 

 -8- 
 In response, GPI again reiterates that Appellants failed to respond to 
the summary judgment motion and made their objections through a motion under 
CR 59.05 only after judgment was entered. GPI asserts it was inappropriate for 
Appellants to raise objections to summary judgment by a post judgment motion 
when the objections should have been raised prior to entry of the judgment. 
II. STANDARD OF REVIEW 
 A court may grant summary judgment “if the pleadings, depositions, 
answers to interrogatories, stipulations, and admissions on file, together with the 
affidavits, if any, show that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and 
that the moving party is entitled to a judgment as a matter of law.” CR 56.03. In 
making that determination, “[t]he record must be viewed in a light most favorable 
to the party opposing the motion for summary judgment and all doubts are to be 
resolved in his favor.” Steelvest, Inc. v. Scansteel Serv. Ctr., Inc., 807 S.W.2d 476, 
480 (Ky. 1991). Summary judgment “is only proper where the movant shows that 
the adverse party could not prevail under any circumstance[].” Paintsville Hosp. 
Co. v. Rose, 683 S.W.2d 255, 256 (Ky. 1985). 
 “The initial burden is on the proponent of the motion for summary 
judgment to convince the trial court of the nonexistence of an issue of material 
fact. Once that burden has been met, the burden shifts to the party opposing 
summary judgment to present affirmative evidence showing a material issue 

 -9- 
exists.” Smothers v. Baptist Hosp. East, 468 S.W.3d 878, 885 (Ky. App. 2015). A 
“properly supported summary judgment motion” cannot be defeated unless the 
opponent presents “at least some affirmative evidence showing that there is a 
genuine issue of material fact for trial.” Steelvest, 807 S.W.2d at 482. 
 Because “[a] motion for summary judgment presents only questions 
of law and a determination of whether a disputed material issue of fact exists,” the 
review is de novo. Patton v. Bickford, 529 S.W.3d 717, 723 (Ky. 2016) (internal 
quotation marks and citations omitted). 
 We review a circuit court’s ruling on a motion to alter, am

leads.caseName: Eugene McNabb v. Orion Township
leads.text:
If this opinion indicates that it is “FOR PUBLICATION,” it is subject to revision 
until final publication in the Michigan Appeals Reports. 

-1- 
S T A T E O F M I C H I G A N 

C O U R T O F A P P E A L S 

EUGENE MCNABB, 

 Plaintiff-Appellant, 

UNPUBLISHED 
November 13, 2026 
10:39 AM 
v No. 371903 
Oakland Circuit Court 
ORION TOWNSHIP, AL DAISLEY, DAVID 
GOODLOE, and DAN’S EXCAVATING, INC., 

LC No. 2019-177748-CZ 
 Defendants-Appellees. 

Before: GADOLA, C.J., and O’BRIEN and MARIANI, JJ. 

PER CURIAM. 
 Plaintiff appeals as of right the trial court’s final opinion and order that dismissed plaintiff’s 
claims against defendants Orion Township (the Township), Al Daisley, David Goodloe, and Dan’s 
Excavating, Inc. Plaintiff on appeal also challenges an earlier order entered by the trial court that 
dismissed two of plaintiff’s other claims. For the reasons explained in this opinion, we affirm. 
I. BACKGROUND 
 Plaintiff owns property, referred to as Lots 9 and 10, adjacent to a sand and gravel mining 
operation (the pit) in the Township. The pit originated during the construction of I -75. After I -75 
was built, Bob Warren of Bob Warren Trucking assumed operation of the pit and entered into an 
informal arrangement with plaintiff to list plaintiff’s property as part of the permit needed to mine the 
pit. After 2006, Dan’s Excavating assumed ownership of the pit and held the permit to mine it. But 
Dan’s Excavating and plaintiff did not continue the informal arrangement that plaintiff had with the 
prior owners of the pit, which eventually led to a series of lawsuits and appeals that generally centered 
around how Dan’s Excavating went about filling and restoring both the pit and the portion of 
plaintiff’s property that was covered by earlier permits to mine the pit. 
In 2008, plaintiff and his wife initiated and settled an action against D an’s Excavating and 
two nonparties. See McNabb v Orion Twp, unpublished per curiam opinion of the Court of Appeals, 
issued December 28, 2021 (Docket No. 354297) (McNabb II), p 1 (discussing history of dispute). In 
2011, plaintiff and his wife initiated another action , this one against Dan’s Excavating and the 
Township, which alleged “that while defendant Dan’s Excavating, Inc. was in the process of filling 

-2- 
and restoring the pit it 1) overfilled certain areas in excess of the permitted elevation; and 2) failed to 
engage in progressive restoration of the pit in violation of defendant Township of Orion’s ‘Earth 
Balancing & Excavation Ordinance,’ referred to as Ordinance 99, and the permit issued thereunder.” 
McNabb v Dan’s Excavating, Inc , unpublished per curiam opinion of the Court of Appeals, issued 
October 14, 2014 (Docket No. 315941) (McNabb I), p 1. Plaintiff ’s complaint in this 2011 action 
“sought damages and mandatory injunctive relief against Dan’s Excavating to remedy the alleged 
violations of the ordinance and mandamus relief against the Township to compel enforcement of 
Ordinance 99 and the permit.” Id. The trial court in the 2011 action granted the defendants’ motions 
for summary disposition on all of the claims alleged in plaintiff’s complaint, and this Court affirmed. 
Id. 
 In 2015, after this Court affirmed the dismissal of plaintiff’s second action, the Township 
amended Ordinance 99 to add a requirement for permittees to maintain activity logs and take 
photographs of each truckload of fill, and plaintiff filed the instant action in 2019 based largely on 
these newly added requirements. McNabb II, unpub op at 2. Plaintiff later amended his complaint to 
include Daisley (a Township code enforcement officer) and Goodloe (a Township building official) 
in their individual capacities as “Township Zoning Enforcement Officers.” Id. Thereafter, a ll 
defendants moved for summary disposition under MCR 2.116(C)(7) and (8), arguing that plaintiff’s 
claims were barred by res judicata. Id. The trial court granted the motions and denied plaintiff’s 
request to file a second amended complaint. Id. 
 Plaintiff appealed, and this Court affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded for further 
proceedings. Id. at 1. This Court held that res judicata did not bar plaintiff’s claims against Daisley 
and Goodloe because they were not parties to any prior action and did not have privity with any 
defendants in those actions. Id. at 5. This Court further held that res judicata did not bar plaintiff’s 
claims premised on the 2015 amendment to Ordinance 99 because those claims could not have been 
brought in 2011 before the amendment was enacted. Id. at 5-6. But this Court upheld the trial court’s 
refusal to allow plaintiff to amend his complaint to add a trespass claim against Dan’s Excavating 
because that claim would be barred by res judicata —this Court explained that the “trespasses 
allegedly committed by [Dan’s Excavating took place] in the years 2001 through 2006,” so plaintiff 
could have asserted those claims in either of his prior actions through the exercise of reasonable 
diligence. Id. at 8. 
 When the case returned to the trial court, that court allowed plaintiff to file an amended 
complaint alleging nine counts against defendants. The court later struck two claims (a declaratory-
judgment claim and a trespass claim) in which plaintiff alleged that Dan’s Excavating was required 
to restore a portion of plaintiff’s property (Lot 10). The court reasoned that the claims related to the 
pre-2015-amendment version of Ordinance 99, and the court interpreted McNabb II to mean that, as 
far as Ordinance 99 was concerned, only plaintiff’s claims alleging violations of the amended portion 
of Ordinance 99 were not barred by res judicata. Plaintiff later conceded that another claim that asked 
the trial court to take superin tending control of the Township’s enforcement of Ordinance 99 was 
moot and no longer viable. 
 The parties eventually filed various motions for summary disposition regarding how to 
dispose of the remaining six claims, and the trial court resolved those motions in an 18-page written 
opinion and order. The trial court concluded that plaintiff’s motion for summary disposition should 

-3- 
be denied and defendants’ motions for summary disposition should be granted, and the court 
accordingly dismissed all of plaintiff’s claims. 
 This appeal followed. 
II. RES JUDICATA 
 Plaintiff first argues that the trial court erred by dismissing his declaratory -judgment and 
trespass claims (Counts I and IX, respectively) on the basis of res judicata. 
A. STANDARD OF REVIEW 
 Whether res judicata bars a claim presents a question of law, reviewed de novo. King v Munro, 
329 Mich App 594, 599; 944 NW2d 198 (2019). 
B. ANALYSIS 
 The doctrine of res judicata prevents relitigation of a claim and is broadly applied. C-Spine 
Orthopedics, PLLC v Progressive Mich Ins Co , 346 Mich App 197, 203; 12 NW3d 20 (2023) . 
“Courts use the doctrine of res judicata to prevent multiple suits litigating the same cause of action.” 
Id. The doctrine of res judicata “bars a subsequent action when (1) the prior action was decided on 
the merits, (2) both actions involve the same parties or their privies, and (3) the claims in the second 
case were, or could have been, resolved in the first case.” Id. 
To the extent that plaintiff argues that the trial court erred by dismissing Count I of his second 
amended complaint, that argument is not properly before this Court. In Count I of the second 
amended complaint, plaintiff asked the trial court to declare that the Township had a duty to compel 
Dan’s Excavating to restore plaintiff’s property next to the pit . After plaintiff filed this complaint, 
the Township asked the trial court to “clarify” whether it was proper to allow plaintiff to pursue Count 
I following McNabb II . In response , plaintiff “agree[d] that Count I is . . . moot.” With this 
concession in the trial court, plaintiff forfeited the ability to contest on appeal the dismissal of Count 
I of his second amended complaint. See Holmes v Holmes, 281 Mich App 575, 587-588; 760 NW2d 
300 (2008) ( “A party may not take a position in the trial court and subsequently seek redress in an 
appellate court that is based on a position contrary to that taken in the trial court.” ) (quotation marks 
and citation omitted); Marshall Lasser, PC v George, 252 Mich App 104, 109; 651 NW2d 158 (2002) 
(“A party is not allowed to assign as error on appeal something which his or her own counsel deemed 
proper at trial since to do so would permit the party to harbor error as an appellate parachute .”) 
(quotation marks and citation omitted). 
As for Count IX, plaintiff alleged that Dan’s Excavating was required to restore any property 
included in the permit for its mining operation, which included plaintiff’s property, but Dan’s 
Excavating had failed to do so. This argument stems from Orion Township Ordinance 99, § 9(A), 
which provides in pertinent part: 
 All areas within any soil excavation site operating under a single permit shall 
be restored progressively. Restoration shall be in accordance with the plan as 
approved by the Board of Appeals at the time the permit is secured. 

-4- 
Plaintiff contends that Dan’s Excavating previously received a permit for its mining operation that 
included plaintiff’s Lot 10, so pursuant to Ordinance 99, § 9, Dan’s Excavating was required to restore 
plaintiff’s Lot 10. 
 In plaintiff’s 2011 action, he raised this same claim—he alleged in his second amended 
complaint in that action that Dan’s Excavating was required by “Section 9 of Ordinance No. 99” to 
restore any lot “on which Dan’s Excavating Inc. . . . or its predecessor(s)[] engaged in mining,” which 
included plaintiff’s Lot 10. The complaint identified the relevant permit governing this restoration as 
“[t]he Permit granted April 26, 2010,” and alleged that “Dan’s Excavating has failed to engage in the 
restoration mandated by the Permit” as required by Ordinance 99, § 9. The trial court dismissed this 
claim on the merits, and plaintiff did not appeal that dismissal. In plaintiff’s 2014 appeal, this Court 
noted this failure in a footnote and held that it constituted abandonment of the issue: 
 We note that, in addition to the alleged overfilling and lack of restoration 
supporting plaintiffs’ claim for mandamus presented on appeal, plaintiffs also sought 
mandamus relief for alleged noncompliance with specific conditions that the Zoning 
Board of Appeals attached to the 2010/2011 permit issued to Dan’s Excavating. On 
appeal, plaintiffs do not address or present any argument regarding these conditions 
attached to the permit, and thus, plaintiffs have abandoned those claims. Yee v 
Shiawassee Co Bd of Comm’rs , 251 Mich App 379, 406; 651 NW2d 756 (2002). 
[McNabb I, pp 2-3, n 1.] 
It follows that, to the extent that plaintiff contends that this Court’s 2014 opinion supports that 
his Count IX could proceed, plaintiff is mistaken. This Court’s 2014 opinion explicitly held that 
plaintiff had failed to raise on appeal the issue related to Ordinance 99, § 9, thereby abandoning the 
issue. That issue was thus only addressed by the trial court in plaintiff’s 2011 action , and that court 
decided the issue on the merits and dismissed it. Count IX is the same claim that plaintiff failed to 
appeal in 2011.1 Because that claim was decided on the merits by the trial court in plaintiff’s 2011 
action against Dan’s Excavating and the Township, plaintiff cannot relitigate the claim as part of this 
action; the claim is barred by res judicata. See C-Spine Orthopedics, PLLC, 346 Mich App at 203. 
III. SUMMARY DISPOSITION 
 Plaintiff next takes issue with the trial court’s rulings in its opinion and order granting 
summary disposition in favor of defendants. 
A. STANDARD OF REVIEW 
 This Court reviews de novo a trial court’s decision on a motion for summary disposition. El-
Khalil v Oakwood Healthcare, Inc, 504 Mich 152, 159; 934 NW2d 665

Keybank, N.A. v Unknown Successor Trustee(s) of Gay Dygert 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06627 
 November 13, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Fourth Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 KEYBANK, N.A., PLAINTIFF-APPELLANT, 
 v 
 UNKNOWN SUCCESSOR TRUSTEE(S) OF GAY DYGERT IF LIVING, AND IF HE/SHE BE DEAD, ANY AND ALL PERSONS UNKNOWN TO PLAINTIFF, CLAIMING, OR WHO MAY CLAIM TO HAVE AN INTEREST IN, OR GENERAL OR SPECIFIC LIEN UPON THE REAL PROPERTY DESCRIBED IN THIS ACTION, ET AL., DEFENDANTS-RESPONDENTS. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Fourth Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 13, 2026 
 660 CA 25-01011 
 Present: Whalen, P.J., Bannister, Nowak, Hannah, And Skinner, JJ. 

 GROSS POLOWY LLC, WILLIAMSVILLE (STEVEN ROSENFELD OF COUNSEL), FOR PLAINTIFF-APPELLANT. 

 Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Onondaga County (Danielle M. Fogel, J.), entered April 17, 2025, in a mortgage foreclosure action. The order dismissed the amended complaint. 
[*1]
 It is hereby ORDERED that the order so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs. 
 Memorandum: Plaintiff commenced this action seeking, among other things, to foreclose on a mortgage secured by a property owned by the Gay T. Dygert Living Trust and to vacate an allegedly erroneous satisfaction of mortgage previously filed by plaintiff with respect to that property. Plaintiff appeals from an order of Supreme Court entered following a limited nonjury trial before a Judicial Hearing Officer (JHO) that, among other things, dismissed the amended complaint. We affirm. 
 Contrary to plaintiff's contention, the court did not err in refusing to grant plaintiff a default judgment ( see Cary v Cimino , 128 AD3d 1460, 1460-1461 [4th Dept 2015]). A plaintiff's entitlement to a default judgment requires submission of " 'proof of service of the summons and the complaint, the facts constituting the claim, and [the] defendant[s'] default' " ( Sutton v Williamsville Suburban , LLC , 174 AD3d 1467, 1468 [4th Dept 2019], lv dismissed 34 NY3d 1091 [2020]; see CPLR 3215 [f]; Woodson v Mendon Leasing Corp. , 100 NY2d 62, 70 [2003]; Rand Constr. Corp. v Cowboys Saloon Syracuse , LLC , 184 AD3d 1206, 1207 [4th Dept 2020]). Although a defendant's default constitutes an admission of all factual allegations in a complaint, "it does not follow that the trial court has a mandatory, ministerial duty to grant a motion for a default judgment upon every properly verified complaint—however deficient—upon which there has been a default" ( Matter of Dyno v Rose , 260 AD2d 694, 698 [3d Dept 1999], appeal dismissed 93 NY2d 998 [1999], lv denied 94 NY2d 753 [1999]; see CPLR 3215 [f]). Instead, whether by verified complaint or a supporting affidavit, a plaintiff must set forth the facts establishing a claim ( see CPLR 3215 [f]; Rand Constr. Corp. , 184 AD3d at 1207; [*2] Dyno , 260 AD2d at 698). 
 " 'When considering an application for a default judgment, it is incumbent upon the court to examine the proof submitted pursuant to CPLR 3215 (f) and determine whether a viable cause of action exists' " ( Booker v McMindes , 220 AD3d 1026, 1027 [3d Dept 2023], lv dismissed 41 NY3d 962 [2024]). "The legal conclusions to be drawn from the applicant's complaint and factual allegations are reserved for the court's determination, and the court retains the discretionary obligation to determine whether the applicant has met the burden of stating a prima facie cause of action" ( Dyno , 260 AD2d at 698). Here, plaintiff failed to submit in support of its motion for, inter alia, a default judgment proof of the facts supporting its claim that the prior satisfaction of mortgage was erroneously issued ( see CPLR 3215 [f]; Rand Constr. Corp. , 184 AD3d at 1207). The amended complaint was not verified and, in any event, contained only a conclusory allegation that the satisfaction of mortgage was erroneously filed ( see Cary , 128 AD3d at 1460-1461; see generally Izmirligil v Steven J. Baum , P.C. , 180 AD3d 767, 770 [2d Dept 2020], lv dismissed in part & denied in part 39 NY3d 956 [2022]). Moreover, the supporting affidavit of plaintiff's banking officer failed to address the satisfaction of mortgage. Inasmuch as "[a] plaintiff's 'failure to submit the proof required by CPLR 3215 (f) should lead a court to deny an application for a default judgment' " ( Rand Constr. Corp. , 184 AD3d at 1207, quoting Manhattan Telecom. Corp. v H & A Locksmith , Inc. , 21 NY3d 200, 203 [2013]), the court properly denied that part of plaintiff's motion seeking a default judgment. 
 Plaintiff further contends that the JHO, to whom the issue whether the satisfaction of mortgage had been erroneously filed had been referred on the parties' consent to hear and determine, erred in determining, after the trial, that there was insufficient evidence that the satisfaction of mortgage was erroneously filed such that the satisfaction of mortgage should be vacated. A verdict in a nonjury civil trial "should not be disturbed upon appeal unless it is obvious that the court's conclusions could not be reached under any fair interpretation of the evidence, especially when the findings of fact rest in large measure on considerations relating to the credibility of witnesses" ( Thoreson v Penthouse Intl ., 80 NY2d 490, 495 [1992], rearg denied 81 NY2d 835 [1993] [internal quotation marks omitted]; see Tarsel v Trombino , 196 AD3d 1100, 1101 [4th Dept 2021]; Livingston v State of New York , 129 AD3d 1660, 1660 [4th Dept 2015], lv denied 26 NY3d 903 [2015]). Moreover, when conducting our review, we must view the record "in the light most favorable to sustain the [order or] judgment" ( Farace v State of New York , 266 AD2d 870, 871 [4th Dept 1999]; see Burke v Women Gynecology & Childbirth Assoc. , P.C. , 195 AD3d 1393, 1394 [4th Dept 2021]). Here, plaintiff's sole witness testified that he was not part of the internal review team that reviewed the relevant account and made the determination with respect to the satisfaction of mortgage, and further testified that he did not have access to the records of that review team. The JHO's determinations that the witness lacked personal knowledge of the facts relevant to plaintiff's filing of the satisfaction of mortgage and that plaintiff therefore failed to submit evidence sufficient to warrant vacatur of the satisfaction of mortgage are therefore supported by a "fair interpretation of the evidence" and should not be disturbed ( Thoreson , 80 NY2d at 495 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see Unger v Ganci [appeal No. 2], 200 AD3d 1604, 1605 [4th Dept 2021]). 
 Entered: November 13, 2026 
 Ann Dillon Flynn 
 Clerk of the Court

 IN THE MATTER OF PINE VIEW CIRCLE, LLC, PETITIONER-RESPONDENT, 
 v 
 MIKELA ATHERTON, RESPONDENT-APPELLANT. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Fourth Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 13, 2026 
 663 CA 25-00928 
 Present: Whalen, P.J., Bannister, Nowak, Hannah, And Skinner, JJ. 

 LEGAL ASSISTANCE OF WESTERN NEW YORK, INC., GENEVA (CANDICE BAKER LEIT OF COUNSEL), FOR RESPONDENT-APPELLANT. 
 CHENEY LAW FIRM, PLLC, GENEVA (DAVID D. BENZ OF COUNSEL), FOR PETITIONER-RESPONDENT. 

 Appeal from an order of the Seneca County Court (Barry L. Porsch, J.), entered June 2, 2025, in a summary eviction proceeding. The order affirmed an order and judgment of the Tyre Town Court. 
[*1]
 It is hereby ORDERED that the order so appealed from is unanimously reversed on the law without costs, the petition filed August 14, 2024, is dismissed and the warrants of eviction issued on that petition are vacated. 
 Memorandum: On August 14, 2024, petitioner, a landlord, filed a petition in Tyre Town Court in this summary holdover eviction proceeding (holdover proceeding) seeking, inter alia, a warrant removing respondent as a tenant based on her alleged failure to annually recertify her income as required by her lease. Following an appearance, Town Court granted the petition and issued a warrant of eviction dated August 28, 2024. Respondent appealed to Seneca County Court, which issued a stay of the warrant pending its determination of the appeal. Subsequently, County Court issued an order that affirmed Town Court's order and judgment and directed Town Court to issue a warrant of eviction; Town Court then issued a new warrant of eviction dated June 5, 2025. 
 In March 2025—during the pendency of the holdover proceeding—petitioner commenced a separate, summary nonpayment eviction proceeding (nonpayment proceeding) in Town Court, alleging in the verified petition that petitioner and respondent entered into a lease agreement, and that "[respondent] has failed to honor her payment obligations under the [a]greement" for the months of April 2024 through March 2025. The nonpayment proceeding terminated in an order and judgment in favor of petitioner, entered in June 2025, from which respondent has not appealed. 
 Respondent now appeals to this Court from County Court's order in the holdover proceeding, contending that reversal is warranted based on petitioner's actions in filing and pursuing the nonpayment proceeding. We agree. 
 "Generally, if a landlord initiates a holdover proceeding and then commences a nonpayment proceeding, the nonpayment case operates as a waiver of the right to proceed with the holdover because it reaffirms the tenancy" ( Third Lenox Terrace Assoc. v Jones , 19 Misc 3d 1103[A] , 2008 NY Slip Op 50493[U] , *1 [Civ Ct, NY County 2008]; see Associated Blind Hous. Dev. Fund Corp. v Katz , 161 AD2d 512, 512-513 [1st Dept 1990]). Not only do "the affirmative acts involved in commencing the nonpayment summary proceeding . . . reaffirm[ the] tenancy, but the existence of the nonpayment petition itself . . . is documentary proof of the existence of [the] tenancy" ( Ansonia Assoc. v Pearlstein , 122 Misc 2d 566, 569 [Civ Ct, NY County 1984]). 
 Here, "[o]nce [petitioner] obtained a final judgment for unpaid rent in the nonpayment proceeding, it was conclusively determined that a valid lease existed between the parties" and, under these circumstances, we conclude that "dismissal of the holdover proceeding [is] proper" ( Blenheim Trading Corp. v Zitomer Pharm. , 191 AD2d 333, 334 [1st Dept 1993]). Inasmuch as the nonpayment proceeding cannot be maintained in the absence of a landlord-tenant relationship, and the nonpayment proceeding was commenced after the issuance of the warrant of eviction in the earlier holdover proceeding, "[petitioner] waived its right to maintain the holdover proceeding" ( Associated Blind Hous. Dev. Fund Corp. , 161 AD2d at 512-513 ). 
 Respondent's remaining contentions are academic in light of the foregoing. 
 Entered: November 13, 2026 
 Ann Dillon Flynn 
 Clerk of the Court

JUSTICE TRUMP, deeming himself disqualified, did not participate in the decision of 
this case. 
 
JUDGE D. ANDREW McMUNN, sitting by temporary assignment. 
 
 
SYLLABUS BY THE COURT 
1. “In reviewing an Intermediate Court of Appeals’ decision from a 
circuit court’s grant of a motion to dismiss, this Court applies a de novo standard of 
review.” Syl. Pt. 1, Folse v. Rollyson, 251 W. Va. 566, 915 S.E.2d 344 (2025).  
2. “Appellate review of a circuit court’s order granting a motion to 
dismiss a complaint is de novo.” Syl. Pt. 2, State ex rel. McGraw v. Scott Runyan Pontiac-
Buick, Inc., 194 W. Va. 770, 461 S.E.2d 516 (1995). 
3. “The constitutionality of a statute is a question of law which this Court 
reviews de novo.” Syl. Pt. 1, State v. Rutherford, 223 W. Va. 1, 672 S.E.2d 137 (2008). 
4. “When the constitutionality of a statute is questioned every reasonable 
construction of the statute must be resorted to by a court in order to sustain constitutionality, 
and any doubt must be resolved in favor of the constitutionality of the legislative 
enactment.” Syl. Pt. 3, Willis v. O’Brien, 151 W. Va. 628, 153 S.E.2d 178 (1967). 
5. “In due recognition of fundamental principles relating to the 
separation of powers among the legislative, executive and judicial branches of government, 
courts recognize the power of the legislature to make reasonable classifications for 
legislative purposes. Courts are bound by a presumption that legislative classifications are 
reasonable, proper and based on a sound exercise of the legislative prerogative. If a statute 
enacted by the legislature applies throughout the state and to all persons, entities or things 
within a class, and if such classification is not arbitrary or unreasonable, the statute must 
 
 
be regarded as general rather than special. In making classifications for legislative 
purposes, a wide range of discretion must be conceded by the courts to the legislature. In 
any case of doubt, courts must favor a construction of a statute which will result in a statute 
being regarded as general rather than special. A statute must be regarded as general rather 
than special when it operates uniformly on all persons, entities or things of a class. A law 
which operates uniformly upon all persons, entities or things as a class is a general law; 
while a law which operates differently as to particular persons, entities or things within a 
class is a special law.” Syl. Pt. 7, State ex rel. Appalachian Power Co. v. Gainer , 149 W. 
Va. 740, 143 S.E.2d 351 (1965). 
6. “A basic purpose of Article VI, Section 39 of the Constitution of West 
Virginia is to preserve uniformity and consistency in the statutory enactments of this State.” 
Syl. Pt. 1, State ex rel. Taxpayers Protective Ass’n of Raleigh Cnty. v. Hanks, 157 W. Va. 
350, 201 S.E.2d 304 (1973). 
 
1 
 
WOOTON, Justice: 
In this appeal from the Intermediate Court of Appeals (“ICA”), the 
petitioners are several citizens of the Town of Harpers Ferry 1 who challenge the 
constitutionality of West Virginia Code § 5B-1-9 (2020) (“the Act”). The respondents 
defending the constitutionality of the Act are Matt Herridge, the current Secretary of the 
Department of Commerce, and Todd Hooker, the acting Executive Director of the West 
Virginia Division of Economic Development. The Circuit Court of Kanawha County 
entered an order that rejected the petitioners’ constitutional challenges; that order was 
affirmed in the ICA decision on appeal. 
After consideration of the parties’ briefs and oral argument, and the record 
on appeal, we find no error. As we discuss below, we affirm the circuit court and ICA’s 
decisions. 
I. FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND 
In 2004, the Legislature adopted the “Tourism Development Act” with the 
goal of promoting “the general welfare and material well-being of the citizens of the state” 
through “the creation or expansion of tourism development projects[.]” W. Va. Code § 5B-
 
1 Those plaintiff-petitioners are Alexander Fleming, Carole Carter, Carol 
Gallant, Barbara Humes, and Benjamin Buckley. Roberta Mead was a plaintiff below who 
chose not to participate in the appeal because she filed to run for a seat on the Harpers Ferry 
Town Council. 
2 
 
2E-2 (2004). The Tourism Development Act permits the qualifying developers of new or 
expanded tourism projects to seek certain tax credits from the respondents. 
In 2020, the Legislature adopted the Act at issue in this case, which the 
parties refer to as the “Tourism Development District Act,” West Virginia Code § 5B-1-9. 
The Act seeks “to induce and assist in tourism development in small municipalities through 
the creation of tourism development districts[.]” W. Va. Code § 5B-1-9(b). Distilled down 
to its essence, the Act permits the respondents to approve the creation of a “tourism 
development district” to encompass projects qualified under the Tourism Development 
Act. Those new or expanded tourism projects within the district are thereafter virtually 
immunized from local regulations, including municipal zoning and land use ordinances, 
municipal regulations on the sale of liquor, beer, or wine, and municipal building codes. 2 
 
2 West Virginia Code § 5B-1-9(l) provides: 
. . . [N]otwithstanding any provision of this code to the 
contrary, or any municipality’s home rule powers with respect 
to ordinances and ordinance procedures, including any 
authority pursuant to the Municipal Home Rule Program under 
§8-1-5a of this code, designated tourism development districts, 
and the tourism development projects or tourism development 
expansion projects therein, may not be subject to the following: 
(1) Municipal zoning, historic preservation, horticultural, 
noise, viewshed, lighting, development, or land use 
ordinances, restrictions, limitations, or approvals; 
(2) Municipal regulation of the sale of alcoholic liquor, 
nonintoxicating beer, or wine for consumption within the 
tourism development district; 
Continued . . . 
3 
 
Moreover, the Act expressly prohibits municipalities “from enacting, adopting, 
implementing, or enforcing ordinances, regulations, or rules” which impede new and 
expanded tourism projects within a district. W. Va. Code § 5B-1-9(c). Instead, the tourism 
development district is subject to building code, land use and other regulations monitored 
by the respondents. See W. Va. Code R. § 145-16-9.2.2 (2026). 
This case arises from limitations imposed by the Act on the creation of 
tourism development districts. First, the Act only applies to new or expanded tourism 
projects “which are located in, or partially in, municipalities with a population of 2,000 or 
less[.]” W. Va. Code § 5B-1-9(a). Second, tourism development districts may only be 
created for projects “with aggregate projected costs of construction, reconstruction, 
 
(3) Municipal building permitting, inspection, or code 
enforcement; 
(4) Municipal license requirements; 
(5) The legal jurisdiction of the municipality in which the 
tourism development district is entirely or partially located, 
except as specifically provided in this article; 
(6) The implementation of any tax, fee, or charge by the 
municipality, except as specifically provided in this section; or 
(7) Any requirement under state law for the consent or approval 
of the municipality in which the tourism development district 
is entirely or partially located of any state or county action 
pursuant to this code, specifically including, but not limited to, 
§7-11B-1 et seq. of this code, for formal consent of the 
governing body of a municipality for county or state action 
regarding the establishment of tax increment financing 
development or redevelopment districts or the approval of tax 
increment financing development or redevelopment plans. 
4 
 
restoration, rehabilitation, or upgrading of not less than $25 million[.]” W. Va. Code § 5B-
1-9(d). Third, the respondents are permitted to approve no more than five tourism 
development districts in the State. W. Va. Code § 5B-1-9(j). 
Since adoption of the Act in 2020, only one tourism development project has 
been approved as a tourism development district. In 2007, a company known as SWaN Hill 
Top House, LLC (“SWaN”) bought the century-old, historic, derelict Hill Top House Hotel 
in Harpers Ferry with the goal of reconstructing it into a luxury hotel. The project 
languished for over a decade, but when SWaN began moving forward with the project in 
2019, friction developed with residents of Harpers Ferry. Soon thereafter, the Legislature 
adopted the Act and SWaN’s Hill Top House development project became the only 
applicant and recipient of a tourism development district designation from the respondents. 
SWaN said it intends to spend more than $138 million redeveloping the hotel. 
The petitioners are citizens, residents, and registered voters in Harpers Ferry. 
According to the most recent Census, in 2020 the Town of Harpers Ferry had a population 
of 269 residents. In January 2022, the petitioners filed a complaint in the Circuit Court of 
Kanawha County against the respondents challenging the constitutionality of the Act. 
Specifically, the petitioners alleged that the Act violates the prohibitions on special laws 
contained in Article VI, §§ 39 and 39a, and violates equal protection principles contained 
in Article III, § 10, all within the West Virginia Constitution. The petitioners also asserted 
that, by transferring political control and power of the Town of Harpers Ferry to a private 
entity, the Act negates the plaintiffs’ right to self-rule guaranteed under the West Virginia 
5 
 
Constitution by Article III, §§ 1, 2, and 3, and Article VI, §§ 39 and 39a; and negates their 
right to vote, guaranteed by Article VI, § 1. 3  The respondents moved to dismiss the 
petitioners’ complaint. 
In an order dated March 29, 2023, the circuit court granted the respondents’ 
motion to dismiss. The circuit court found the Act had a rational basis when it created a 
class of large tourism development projects located in West Virginia’s smallest 
municipalities and had a reasonable relationship to the policy goals outlined in the Act, and 
so found it did not violate equal protection principles or the constitutional prohibition on 
special laws. Further, the court found no guaranteed right to “self-rule” in the Constitution 
and found no “right to vote” was violated because municipalities have no inherent powers, 
only those granted to them by the Legislature.4 
 
3 The petitioners also alleged that the Act attempts to bind future legislatures 
by providing for the perpetual existence of tourism development districts for 99 years, in 
violation of Article VI of the West Virginia Constitution. The circuit court found the Act

Shearing v Town of Gates 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06619 
 November 13, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Fourth Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 KELLY SHEARING, PLAINTIFF-APPELLANT, 
 v 
 TOWN OF GATES AND GATES POLICE DEPARTMENT, DEFENDANTS-RESPONDENTS. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Fourth Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 13, 2026 
 623 CA 25-00768 
 Present: Curran, J.P., Montour, Ogden, Delconte, And Skinner, JJ. 

 DOLCE PANEPINTO, P.C., BUFFALO (KAYLA E. LEONARD OF COUNSEL), FOR PLAINTIFF-APPELLANT. 
 GERBER CIANO KELLY BRADY LLP, GARDEN CITY (BRENDAN T. FITZPATRICK OF COUNSEL), FOR DEFENDANTS-RESPONDENTS. 

 Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Monroe County (James A. Vazzana, J.), entered April 28, 2025. The order, among other things, granted the motion of defendants for summary judgment dismissing the complaint. 
[*1]
 It is hereby ORDERED that the order so appealed from is modified on the law by denying defendants' motion in part and reinstating the first cause of action against defendant Town of Gates, and as modified the order is affirmed without costs. 
 Memorandum: Plaintiff commenced this premises liability and Labor Law § 200 action seeking damages for injuries she allegedly sustained when she slipped and fell on an accumulation of black ice in a public parking lot owned and operated by defendant Town of Gates (Town). Defendants moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, contending that the action was barred because they had not received prior written notice of the allegedly dangerous condition as required by section 158-32 of the Code of the Town of Gates, that the Labor Law § 200 cause of action was outside the scope of the notice of claim and was without merit, and that defendant Gates Police Department was merely an administrative arm of the Town and thus was not subject to being sued. Plaintiff cross-moved for partial summary judgment on the issues of, inter alia, whether the accumulation of ice in the parking lot constituted a dangerous condition and whether defendants had constructive notice of the condition. Supreme Court determined that defendants did not have prior written notice of the alleged icy condition and that plaintiff did not raise a triable issue of fact regarding the applicability of an exception to the prior written notice requirement. The court therefore granted the motion and denied the cross-motion. Plaintiff appeals. 
 Plaintiff contends that the court erred in granting the motion insofar as it sought summary judgment dismissing the complaint based on the absence of prior written notice. We agree. "[A] publicly-owned parking lot falls within the definition of a 'highway' and therefore prior [written] notice of [a] defect is required" in order to bring a negligence action relating to a defect in a [*2] parking lot against a municipality where, as here, the municipality has enacted a prior written notice requirement as permitted by General Municipal Law § 50-e (4) ( Groninger v Village of Mamaroneck , 17 NY3d 125, 128 [2011]; see generally Brick v City of Niagara Falls , 121 AD3d 1591, 1592 [4th Dept 2014]). A municipality bears the initial burden on its summary judgment motion of establishing that it did not receive prior written notice of the alleged defect ( see DeMaioribus v Town of Cheektowaga , 188 AD3d 1643, 1643 [4th Dept 2020]). The burden then 
 " 'shifts to the plaintiff to demonstrate [the existence of a triable issue of fact as to the requisite written notice or] the applicability of one of [the] two recognized exceptions to the rule—that the municipality affirmatively created the defect through an act of negligence or that a special use resulted in a special benefit to the locality' " ( Horst v City of Syracuse , 191 AD3d 1297, 1297-1298 [4th Dept 2021], quoting Yarborough v City of New York , 10 NY3d 726, 728 [2008]). 
 Contrary to plaintiff's contention, defendants met their initial burden of showing that they did not receive the requisite prior written notice. In support of their motion, defendants submitted the affidavit of the Town Clerk, who averred that the Town had not received written notice of an accumulation of ice or any other hazardous condition in the area of the accident "at any time prior to [p]laintiff's fall." Plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact with respect to that issue. 
 Contrary to plaintiff's further contention, she did not raise a triable issue of fact with respect to the applicability of the special use exception to the prior written notice rule. "The special use exception is reserved for situations where a landowner whose property abuts a public street or sidewalk derives a special benefit from that property unrelated to the public use, and is therefore required to maintain a portion of that property" ( Poirier v City of Schenectady , 85 NY2d 310, 315 [1995]). "A special use is typically characterized by the installation of some object in the sidewalk or street or some variance in the construction thereof" ( Hart v City of Buffalo , 218 AD3d 1140, 1150 [4th Dept 2023]). Here, plaintiff's accident occurred in a parking lot that, although used by staff from the Gates Police Department for parking, was also available to the public for parking. Thus, plaintiff failed to demonstrate that defendants derived any "special benefit from that property unrelated to the public use" ( Poirier , 85 NY2d at 315). 
 We agree with plaintiff, however, that she raised a triable issue of fact with respect to the applicability of the exception for defects created by the municipality. The affirmative creation exception applies where "it can be proven that the 'locality created the defect or hazard through an affirmative act of negligence' " ( San Marco v Village/Town of Mount Kisco , 16 NY3d 111, 116 [2010], rearg denied 16 NY3d 796 [2011], quoting Amabile v City of Buffalo , 93 NY2d 471, 474 [1999]). "While the mere failure to remove all snow or ice from a sidewalk is an act of omission, rather than an affirmative act of negligence, a municipality's act in piling snow as part of its snow removal efforts, which snow pile then melts and refreezes to create a dangerous icy condition, constitutes an affirmative act" ( Gilbert v City of Rye , 175 AD3d 470, 472 [2d Dept 2019] [internal quotation marks omitted]; see generally Brockway v County of Chautauqua , 187 AD3d 1674, 1675 [4th Dept 2020]). Here, we conclude that, "when viewed in the light most favorable to plaintiff and giving her the benefit of every reasonable inference" ( DelRosario v Liverpool Lodging , Inc. , 170 AD3d 1595, 1596 [4th Dept 2019]; see Esposito v Wright , 28 AD3d 1142, 1143 [4th Dept 2006]), the deposition testimony submitted by plaintiff, combined with the opinion of plaintiff's meteorological expert, is sufficient to raise a triable issue of fact whether the Town deliberately pushed snow onto the edge of the sidewalk and whether that snow then melted and refroze to create a dangerous icy condition ( see Gilbert , 175 AD3d at 472; Urban v City of Albany , 90 AD3d 1132, 1134 [3d Dept 2011], lv dismissed 18 NY3d 921 [2012]; Smith v County of Orange , 51 AD3d 1006, 1006 [2d Dept 2008]). 
 Defendants contend, as an alternative ground for partial affirmance ( see Verdugo v Fox [*3] Bldg. Group , Inc. , 218 AD3d 1179, 1181-1182 [4th Dept 2023]; see generally Parochial Bus Sys. v Board of Educ. of City of N.Y. , 60 NY2d 539, 544-545 [1983]), that the motion should be granted insofar as it seeks dismissal of the complaint against the Gates Police Department inasmuch as the Gates Police Department is merely an administrative arm of the Town and, therefore, cannot be independently sued ( see Taylor v City of Buffalo , 229 AD3d 1125, 1125-1126 [4th Dept 2024]; see generally Town Law § 150 [1]). We agree, and we note that "plaintiff did not oppose the motion to that extent" ( Hagenbuch v Victoria Woods HOA , Inc. , 125 AD3d 1520, 1521 [4th Dept 2015]). 
 As a further alternative ground for partial affirmance of the order, defendants contend that the motion should be granted insofar as it seeks summary judgment dismissing plaintiff's second cause of action, for violation of Labor Law § 200. We agree. "Section 200 of the Labor Law is a codification of the common-law duty imposed upon an owner or general contractor to provide construction site workers with a safe place to work" ( Comes v New York State Elec. & Gas Corp. , 82 NY2d 876, 877 [1993]) . Although plaintiff's notice of claim alleged that defendants were negligent in "failing to provide a safe place to work," it included "no allegations, direct or indirect, that [plaintiff] was working [on] . . . a construction project at the time of the accident" ( Washington v City of New York , 190 AD3d 1009, 1011 [2d Dept 2021]). Thus, plaintiff's Labor Law § 200 claim is foreclosed ( see id. ). Moreover, even assuming, arguendo, that the notice of claim provided sufficient notice of a possible Labor Law 
 § 200 claim, we conclude that plaintiff "was not within the class of workers" that Labor Law § 200 was enacted to protect ( Gibson v Worthington Div. of McGraw-Edison Co. , 78 NY2d 1108, 1109 [1991]) inasmuch as plaintiff was not "engaged in construction or manufacturing work at the time of the accident" ( Curran v JJML , Inc. , 240 AD3d 1328, 1331 [4th Dept 2025]; see generally Whelen v Warwick Val. Civic & Social Club , 47 NY2d 970, 971 [1979]; Fuller v Spiesz , 53 AD3d 1093, 1094 [4th Dept 2008]) but was instead in the process of transporting a suspect to the Gates Police Department when she slipped and fell. In light of our conclusions, we modify the order by denying that part of the motion with respect to the first cause of action and reinstating that cause of action against the Town. 
 Contrary to plaintiff's further contention on appeal, the court did not err in denying her cross-motion. With respect to the issue of constructive notice, plaintiff failed to meet her initial burden of establishing that the alleged black ice that caused plaintiff to fall was visible and apparent for a sufficient length of time before the accident to permit the Town to discover and correct it ( see Steffens v Sachem Cent. Sch. Dist. , 190 AD3d 1003, 1005 [2d Dept 2021]; Calabro v Harbour at Blue Point Home Owners Assn. , Inc. , 120 AD3d 462, 463 [2d Dept 2014]; Bullard v Pfohl ' s Tavern , Inc. , 11 AD3d 1026, 1027 [4th Dept 2004]). Further, plaintiff failed to meet her burden of establishing the existence of a dangerous condition as a matter of law. "[W]hether a dangerous or defective condition exists on the property of another so as to create liability depends on the peculiar facts and circumstances of each case . . . [and] the existence or nonexistence of a defect or dangerous condition is generally a question of fact for the jury" ( Wiedenbeck v Lawrence , 170 AD3d 1669, 1669 [4th Dept 2019] [internal quotation marks omitted]; see Trincere v County of Suffolk , 90 NY2d 976, 977 [1997]; Alexander v State of New York , 193 AD3d 1328, 1329 [4th Dept 2021]). 
 All concur except Curran , J.P., who dissents in part and votes to affirm in the following memorandum: I respectfully dissent in part and vote to affirm inasmuch as I conclude that plaintiff has not raised a triable issue of material fact with respect to the applicability of the affirmative creation exception to the prior written notice requirement ( see generally Walters v City of Buffalo , 230 AD3d 1571, 1572 [4th Dept 2024]). In my view, and contrary to the majority's conclusion, the record is devoid of evidence that defendant Town of Gates (Town) "deliberately pushed snow onto the edge of the sidewalk . . . that . . . then melted and refroze to [*4] create [the specific] dangerous icy condition" that caused plaintiff's accident.

On Defendants’ Motion to Dismiss Plaintiffs’ Complaint 
M
arte King, Somers Point, NJ, Pro-Se Plaintiff.

2 

 Plaintiffs are the former occupants of Unit 1407-B at 1407 Saint Elizabeth 
Street, Wilmington Delaware (“ the property”). Plaintiffs have alleged that they 
were exposed to mold at the property. They have filed a complaint sounding in 
negligence, fraudulent concealment, intentional misrepresentation, consumer 
fraud and breach of contract. Plaintiffs have sued two separate sets of Defendants. 
The first set consists of Dunning Properties , LLC, Maureen A . Dunning, and 
Michael C. Dunning (collectively the “Dunning Defendants”). The second set of 
Defendants are Pabian Ventures, LLC, Pabian Property Management, LLC, 
Pabian Properties, LLC and Edward Pabian (collectively the “Pabian 
Defendants”). Both sets of Defendants have filed a motion to dismiss. This is the 
Court’s decision on the motion to dismiss. 
FACTS 
 The following facts are taken from the Complaint and Answers filed. 
 In 2018 Isaiah Baggs entered into a lease agreement for the property with 
the Dunning Defendants. The sole tenant who signed the lease was Isaiah Baggs. 
The lease agreement provided that the maximum number of tenants was one and 
that the “Tenant shall not assign the lease”. 
 The property was sold by the Dunning Defendants to the Pabian Defendants 
on April 1, 2022. 
3 

 Before the Plaintiffs began residing at the property Baggs reported mold 
issues. On May 1, 2024, Baggs vacated the rental unit, but not before receiving 
$1,650 in compensation from Pabian, following mold complaints Baggs raised at 
the end of his tenancy. In exchange for this consideration, Baggs agreed to release 
any claims he otherwise had against Pabian for wrongdoing related to mold, and 
specifically agreed to take “no further legal action or compensation” against 
Pabian. This release indicates that upon signing the release Baggs no longer had 
access to the rental unit. 
 Plaintiffs occupied the property during 2023 through April 11, 2024 , with 
their infant daughter K.K. who was born on September 9, 2023. On March 24, 
2024, a rain event occurred which resulted in leaking into the unit and that 
subsequent testing revealed mold in the property. As a result of their occupancy 
of the property Plaintiffs allege they were exposed to mold which caused personal 
injuries to Marte King and K.K. Plaintiffs vacated the property on April 11, 2024, 
due to the mold. 
PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
 On November 13, 2025, Plaintiffs filed suit against the same Defendants in 
the Court of Chancery.
0F
1 The complaint sought equitable relief, alleged fraudulent 
concealment, sought to pierce the corporate veil, to establish a constructive trust
