and sought an emergency order for preservation of evidence. The underlying basis 
for the complaint was Plaintiffs’ allegations that they were injured from exposure 
to mold in the property. Both sets of Defendants moved for dismissal in the Court 
of Chancery. The Court dismissed the claims against the Dunning Defendants 
based on the statute of limitations and that the fraudulent concealment claim failed 
to state a claim. The Court granted the Plaintiffs’ leave to amend their complaint 
as to the Pabian Defendants. An amended complaint was filed. The Pabian 
Defendants moved to dismiss that complaint for a number of reasons including the 
reasons advanced in the instant motion to dismiss and Plaintiffs opposed. The 
decision in the Court of Chancery remains pending. 
STANDARD OF REVIEW 
When reviewing a Motion to Dismiss under Superior Court Rule 12(b)(6), 
the Court (1) accepts all well- plead factual allegations as true, (2) accepts even 
vague allegations as well-plead if they give the opposing party notice of the claim, 
(3) draws all reasonable inferences in favor of the non-moving party, and (4) only 
dismisses a case where the Plaintiff would not be entitled to recover under any 
reasonably conceivable set of circumstances.1F
2 “Dismissal is warranted where the 
plaintiff has failed to plead facts supporting an element of the claim, or that under 

2 ET Aggregator, LLC v. PFJE Asset Co Holdings LLC, 2023 WL 8535181, at *6 (Del. Super. Dec. 8, 2023). 
5 

no reasonable interpretation of the facts alleged could the complaint state a claim 
for which relief might be granted.”2F
3 
ANALYSIS 
 Plaintiffs’ complaint contains six counts for relief: (1) Negligence, Premises 
Liability, and Gross Negligence, (2) Fraudulent Concealment and Intentional 
Misrepresentation, (3) Delaware Consumer Fraud Act, (4) Breach of Rental 
Agreement and Statutory Landlord Duties, (5) Br each of Quiet Enjoyment and 
Constructive-Eviction Theory of Leasehold Damages, and (6) Punitive Damages. 
THE DUNNING DEFENDANTS 
 The Dunning Defendant s sold the property to the Pabian Defendant s on 
April 1, 2022. The Plaintiffs and Dunning Defendants were strangers to each other 
until the Dunning Defendants were sued in the Court of Chancery action. 
 In order to state a claim based on negligence, gross negligence or premises 
liability a Defendant must owe a legal duty to the Plaintiffs at the relevant time. 
The Dunning Defendants sold the property to the Pabian Defendants on April 1, 
2022. Any claim based on negligence, gross negligence or premises liability 
requires that the Dunning Defendants owed a duty to the Plaintiffs at a relevant 
time. If the Defendants owed a duty to the Plaintiffs that duty arose from the 
Plaintiffs’ occupancy of the property. The Dunning Defendants did not own the 

3 Hedenberg v. Raber, 2004 WL 2191164, at *1 (Del. Super. Aug. 20, 2004). 
6 

property during the Plaintiffs’ occupancy of the premises nor during any relevant 
time they were contemplating living at the property. On this record the Dunning 
Defendants are entitled to summary judgment as to Count 1 of the Complaint. 
 The claims based on fraudulent concealment and the Consumer Fraud Act 
require proof of an affirmative act directly toward the Plaintiff .3F
4 No such 
affirmative act has been alleged in the instant complaint. On this basis the 
Dunning Defendants are entitled to summary judgment on Counts 2 and 3. 
 A breach of contract action action requires that there actually be a contract 
between the parties. Absent a lease agreement Plaintiff s’ count for breach of 
contract fails. The complaint does not allege a lease agreement between the 
Dunning Defendants and the Plaintiff s. A s such the Dunning Defendants are 
entitled to summary judgment as to Count 4 of the complaint. 
 If a claim for breach of the quiet enjoyment of a lease and for constructive 
eviction exists, there has to be a landlord-tenant relationship between the parties. 
A landlord-tenant relationship between Plaintiffs and Dunning Defendants was not 
pled in the complaint (probably because it did not exist). The Dunning Defendants 
are entitled to summary judgment as to Count 4 and 5 of the Complaint. 

4 Renovaro Inc. Gumrukcu, 2025 WL 3134533, at *8-9 (Del. Ch. Nov. 7, 2025); Bromwich v. Hanby, 2010 WL 
8250796, at *6-7 (Del. Super. Jul. 1, 2010). 
7 

 A claim for punitive damages is not an independent cause of action and 
depends on the existence of a separate claim to obtain punitive damages. As the 
Dunning Defendants are entitled to summary judgment on the other claims 
asserted, the punitive damage claim fails as a matter of law. Dunning Defendants 
are entitled to summary judgment on the punitive damage claim and all other 
claims against them. There is no just reason for delay in entering final judgment 
as to the Dunning Defendants. Therefore, pursuant to Superior Court Rule 54(b), 
final judgment is entered as to the Dunning Defendants. 
THE PABIAN DEFENDANTS 
The Pabian Defendants have moved to dismiss the Plaintiff s’ claims for a 
number of reasons. Initially it appears clear Edward Pabian (individually) and 
Pabian Property Management, LLC had no interaction with the Plaintiffs in the 
events surrounding Plaintiffs’ occupation of the property. On this basis the claims 
against them are dismissed. 
 Next, the Pabian Defendants move to dismiss the personal injury claims 
based on the statute of limitations. The statute of limitations for a personal injury 
claim is two years.4F
5 Plaintiffs allege that they occupied the rental until sometime 
in 2023 and moved out in April 2024 due to the mold. The complaint in this case 
was filed on August 26, 2026, well beyond the two year limitations period. 

5 10 Del.C. §8119. 
8 

 Plaintiffs invoke the inherently unknow able injury and fraudulent 
concealment tolling doctrines in response to the Pabian D efendants’ statute of 
limitations defense. Plaintiffs also invoke 10 Del. C. §1902 as well. 
The inherently unknowable tolling doctrine is not applicable when “facts 
exist sufficient to put a person of ordinary intelligence and prudence on inquiry 
which, if pursued, would lead to the discovery of such facts.”5F
6 Plaintiffs have pled 
that “[p]laintiffs observed manifestations of water, moisture, skin injury, and other 
conditions during occupancy . . . .” 6F
7 On this record the inherently unknowable 
tolling doctrine does not apply. 
 The result is similar for the Plaintiffs’ argument that the fraudulent 
concealment doctrine tolls the statute of limitations. In order to toll a statute based 
on fraudulent concealment the d efendant must have actual knowledge of the 
alleged wrong and the defendant must have taken an affirmative act to conceal it.7F
8 
“A defendant’s ‘mere silence is insufficient to establish fraudulent concealment’” 
as a basis for tolling.8F
9 Delaware law requires that the defendant have “done some 
affirmative act or acts involving ‘ actual artifice’ which prevents a plaintiff from 
discovering the facts giving rise to his or her cause of action, ‘or some 

6 Saunders v. Lightwave Logistics, Inc., 2023 WL 4851630, at *2 (Del. Super. Jul. 28, 2023) (quoting Wal-Mart 
Stores, Inc. v. AIG Life Ins. Co., 860 A.2d 312, 319 (Del. 2004)). 
7 ¶ 26. 
8 LGM Holdings, LLC v. Schurder, 340 A.3d 1134, 1146-47 (Del. 2025). 
9 Id. at 1148 (quoting AssuredPartners of Virginia, LLC v. Sheehan, 2020 WL 2789706, at *17 (Del. Super. May 
29, 2020)). 
9 

misrepresentation which is intended to put the plaintiff off the trail of inquiry.’”9F
10 
In the instant case Plaintiffs have not alleged specific or particular facts supporting 
an allegation that the Pabian Defendants took an affirmative act towards them. As 
such the tolling doctrine of fraudulent concealment has not been properly pled. 
 Plaintiffs invoke 10 Del. C. §1902. Section 1902 provides that: 
No civil action, suit or other proceeding brought in any 
court of this State shall be dismissed solely on the ground 
that such court is without jurisdiction of the subject matter, 
either in the original proceeding or on appeal. Such 
proceeding may be trans ferred to an appropriate court for 
hearing and determination, provided that the party 
otherwise adversely affected, within 60 days after the order 
denying the jurisdiction of the first court has become final,

leads.caseName: Dr. Jeff Isaacs v. Google LLC
leads.court: Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
leads.text:
NOT FOR PUBLICATION 

In the 
United States Court of Appeals 
For the Eleventh Circuit 
____________________ 
No. 26-10369 
Non-Argument Calendar 
____________________ 

DR. JEFF ISAACS, 
on behalf of themselves and 
all others similarly situated, 
GREENFLIGHT VENTURE CORPORATION, 
Plaintiﬀs-Appellants, 
versus 

GOOGLE LLC, 
Defendant-Appellee. 
 ____________________ 
Appeal from the United States District Court 
for the Southern District of Florida 
D.C. Docket No. 9:24-cv-80395-KMM 
____________________ 

Before LUCK, LAGOA, and BRASHER, Circuit Judges. 
PER CURIAM: 
USCA11 Case: 26-10369 Document: 48-1 Date Filed: 11/13/2026 Page: 1 of 16 
2 Opinion of the Court 26-10369 
This appeal arises from an antitrust dispute in which Green-
flight Venture Corp. and Dr. Jeff Isaacs allege that Google LLC re-
taliated against Dr. Isaacs for his extensive litigation history against 
non-party Apple Inc. by diminishing the visibility of his website, 
OkCaller, on Google. Greenflight and Dr. Isaacs appeal the district 
court’s grant of Google’s motion to dismiss their second amended 
complaint and denial of Dr. Isaacs’s subsequent Rule 59(e) motion 
to alter or amend judgment, as well as Greenflight’s corresponding 
motion to join Dr. Isaacs’s Rule 59(e) motion. Greenflight and 
Dr. Isaacs present various theories for reversing the district court’s 
decisions. After careful review, we affirm the district court. 
I. 
Dr. Isaacs initiated this case in April 2024 by filing a pro se 
lawsuit against Google predicated on a sole count of patent in-
fringement. The original complaint alleged that Dr. Isaacs founded 
OkCaller.com, a website which employed “reverse phone search 
technology” that enabled individuals who receive a text message 
or phone call to look up the name of an anonymous caller . Dkt. 1 
at ¶¶ 1, 6. The complaint additionally alleged that Google had en-
tered into a partnership with Dr. Isaacs and Greenflight—of which 
Dr. Isaacs served as CEO —as evidenced by their “[r]egular com-
munications.” Id. at ¶ 24. 
In addition to creating OkCaller, Dr. Isaacs developed a 
coronavirus tracking app called “Coronavirus Reporter” in early 
2020. Id. ¶ 11. After non-party Apple Inc. rejected th e app, 
USCA11 Case: 26-10369 Document: 48-1 Date Filed: 11/13/2026 Page: 2 of 16 
26-10369 Opinion of the Court 3 

Dr. Isaacs “became a lead witness in Apple antitrust matters con-
cerning App censorship.” Id. Dr. Isaacs alleges that on the same day 
he submitted a closing brief to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 
Ninth Circuit in an unrelated lawsuit involving Apple, Google ab-
ruptly terminated their so-called partnership. Dr. Isaacs suspected 
that this termination was in retaliation for his litigation against Ap-
ple. After this event, which Dr. Isaacs asserts occurred around 
Thanksgiving 2022, OkCaller “was effectively shut down by 
Google with no warning or explanation, and for no good reason, 
but for [Google]’s anti-competitive and/or retaliatory motives.” Id. 
at ¶¶ 20, 50–51. 
After Google moved to dismiss Dr. Isaacs’s complaint, he 
amended it. The amended complaint rested on similar allegations, 
added Greenflight as a plaintiff, and asserted three antitrust counts 
and two state law counts —in addition to the original patent in-
fringement count —on behalf of both Dr. Isaacs and Greenflight . 
The state law counts and two of the antitrust counts were styled as 
class action claims. Thereafter, the district court: (1) dismissed the 
patent infringement count as asserted by Dr. Isaacs because Green-
flight, not Dr. Isaacs, held the alleged patent at issue; (2) dismissed 
the class action counts as asserted by Dr. Isaacs on the ground that 
a pro se plaintiff may not bring class action counts under the Federal 
Rules of Civil Procedure; and, (3) reasoning that Greenflight suffi-
ciently represented Dr. Isaacs’ interests, severed and stayed the re-
maining non-class-action-antitrust count as asserted by Dr. Isaacs 
pending final resolution of Greenflight’s counts against Google. 
USCA11 Case: 26-10369 Document: 48-1 Date Filed: 11/13/2026 Page: 3 of 16 
4 Opinion of the Court 26-10369 
Google moved to dismiss the amended complaint, which 
the district court granted in part. The district court permitted 
Dr. Isaacs and Greenflight one final opportunity to amend their 
complaint, and on December 17, 2024, they filed a second amended 
complaint. 
The second amended complaint —which is the operative 
complaint—contained five counts: four counts under sections 1 
and 2 of the Sherman Act, 15 U.S.C. §§ 1–2; and one count under 
California’s Unfair Competition Law, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code 
§ 17200. Google moved to dismiss the operative complaint, argu-
ing that each count failed to state a claim upon which relief could 
be granted. The district court agreed with Google. Construing the 
operative complaint as asserting counts on behalf of Greenflight, 
represented by counsel, and Dr. Isaacs, proceeding pro se, the dis-
trict court dismissed all of Greenflight’s counts with prejudice and 
ordered Dr. Isaacs to show cause “why his pro se claim(s) should 
not be dismissed for the same reasons Greenflight’s (identical) an-
titrust [counts] were dismissed.” Dkt. 65 at 20. It later dismissed 
Dr. Isaacs’s counts as well. 
Following the dismissal of the operative complaint with 
prejudice, Dr. Isaacs and Greenflight sought a hearing to address 
Google’s reply to the motion to dismiss, or for the court to recon-
sider its dismissal. The district court denied this motion. 
Then, Dr. Isaacs moved pro se for reconsideration of the op-
erative complaint’s dismissal under Federal Rule of Civil Proce-
USCA11 Case: 26-10369 Document: 48-1 Date Filed: 11/13/2026 Page: 4 of 16 
26-10369 Opinion of the Court 5 

dure 59(e). Twenty days later, Greenflight moved to join and sup-
port Dr. Isaacs’s Rule 59(e) motion. The district court denied both 
motions. 
This appeal followed. 
II. 
We review the district court’s grant of a motion to dismiss 
for failure to state a claim de novo. Swinford v. Santos, 121 F.4th 179, 
186 (11th Cir. 2024). We likewise review issues of antitrust standing 
de novo. Sunbeam Television Corp. v. Neilsen Media Rsch., Inc., 711 F.3d 
1264, 1270 (11th Cir. 2013). Moreover, we review the district 
court’s denial of a motion for reconsider ation for abuse of discre-
tion. Richardson v. Johnson, 598 F.3d 734, 740 (11th Cir. 2010). 
III. 
Dr. Isaacs and Greenflight assert eleven grounds for reversal. 
We need not consider all the issues raised so long as there exists 
any ground in the record to support affirmance of the district 
court’s decision. See Blackman v. United Cap. Invs., Inc., 12 F.3d 1030, 
1033 (11th Cir. 1994); Lucas v. W.W. Grainger, Inc., 257 F.3d 1249, 
1256 (11th Cir. 2001) (quoting Jaffke v. Dunham, 352 U.S. 280, 281 
(1957)). Accordingly, we discuss each dispositive issue below. 
A. 
Dr. Isaacs and Greenflight argue that the district court erred 
in granting Google’s motion to dismiss the operative complaint for 
failure to state a claim. We conclude it did not. 
USCA11 Case: 26-10369 Document: 48-1 Date Filed: 11/13/2026 Page: 5 of 16 
6 Opinion of the Court 26-10369 
1. 
Apart from plausibly pleading an antitrust injury, a private 
plaintiff raising an antitrust injury must establish antitrust standing. 
Mun. Utils. Bd. of Albertville v. Ala. Power Co., 934 F.2d 1493, 1498–99 
(11th Cir. 1991). Antitrust standing requires a plaintiff to establish 
(1) that it has suffered an antitrust injury, “which is to say injury of 
the type that the antitrust laws were intended to prevent and that 
flows from that which makes the defendants’ acts unlawful”; and 
(2) that “it is an efficient enforcer of the antitrust laws.” Fla. Seed Co. 
v. Monsanto Co., 105 F.3d 1372, 1374 (11th Cir. 1997). 
The second prong is analyzed through the “target area test,” 
which “r equires that an antitrust plaintiff both ‘ prove that he is 
within that sector of the economy endangered by a breakdown of 
competitive conditions in a particular industry ’ and that he is ‘ the 
target against which anticompetitive activity is directed. ’” Id. 
(quoting Nat’l Indep. Theatre Exhibitors, Inc. v. Buena Vista Distrib. 
Co., 748 F.2d 602, 608 (11th Cir. 1984)). “ Basically, a plaintiff must 
show that it is a customer or competitor in the relevant antitrust 
market.” Id. And “[w]hether or not the plaintiff is a customer or a 
competitor, in order to meet the second prong, the plaintiff must 
prove the existence of a competitor willing and able to enter the 
relevant market, but for the exclusionary conduct of the incumbent 
monopolist.” Sunbeam Television Corp., 711 F.3d at 1273. 
The operative complaint alleges Google maintains a monop-
oly in the “general search engine services” market. Dkt. 61 at 
USCA11 Case: 26-10369 Document: 48-1 Date Filed: 11/13/2026 Page: 6 of 16 
26-10369 Opinion of the Court 7 

¶¶ 104–06. Greenflight’s and Dr. Isaacs’s antitrust standing is pred-
icated on the allegation that OkCaller is a competitor to Google 
and that Greenflight and Dr. Isaacs are “consumers of Google[’s] 
[general search engine] platform through their provision of content 
like [Google webmaster tools].” Id. at ¶ 107 (citation modified). 
On these allegations , Appellants fail to satisfy the second 
prong for antitrust standing because they have not plausibly 
demonstrated that they are “efficient enforcer[s] of the antitrust 
laws.” Fla Seed Co., 105 F.3d at 1374. First, the operative complaint 
alleges that OkCaller operates as a “specialized search” website. Id. 
at ¶¶ 4–5, 13, 20, 68. Nowhere does it allege that OkCaller operates 
in the general search engine services market or plead direct com-
petition between OkCaller and Google in that market. Greenflight 
and Dr. Isaacs thus fail to show that OkCaller is a “ competitor in 
the relevant antitrust market.” Fla. Seed Co., 105 F.3d at 1374. Sec-
ond, the operative complaint alleges in conclusory fashion that 
“Google engages in anticompetitive conduct to monopolize inter-
net search” and “has substantially foreclosed competition in gen-
eral search . . . services.” Dkt. 61 at ¶¶ 8, 88. But it does not suffi-
ciently allege how, exactly, Google is preventing OkCaller from 
competing in the general search engine services market . See Ash-
croft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (“[A] complaint must contain 
sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to ‘state a claim to relief 
that is plausible on its face.’” (quoting Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 
U.S. 544, 570 (2007)). Third, a plaintiff, regardless of whether he is 
advancing a customer- or competitor-based antitrust injury, must 
USCA11 Case: 26-10369 Document: 48-1 Date Filed: 11/13/2026 Page: 7 of 16 
8 Opinion of the Court 26-10369 
prove a willing-and-able competitor would have entered the rele-
vant market had the monopolist not engaged in anticompetitive 
behavior. Sunbeam Television Corp., 711 F.3d at 1273. The operative 
complaint does not, however, identify, let alone plausibly allege, 
that a competitor was willing and able to enter the general search 
engine services market but for Google’s exclusionary conduct. 
Greenflight and Dr. Isaacs attempt to circumvent this plead-
ing deficiency by arguing that Google is a “multi- sided platform” 
as recognized by the Supreme Court in Ohio v. Am. Express Co., 585 
U.S. 529 (2018). Doc. 25 at 14–15. The Court’s opinion in American 
Express Co. concerned credit-card networks, which the Court de-
scribed as two-sided platforms because they “offer[] different prod-
ucts or services to two different groups who both depend on the 
platform to intermediate between them.” 585 U.S. at 534. Credit-
card networks extend credit to cardholders, “which allows them to 
make purchases without cash and to defer payment until later,” 
and allows merchants “to avoid the cost of processing transactions 
and offers them quick, guaranteed payment.” Id. ; se

leads.caseName: Jackson v. Ventavia Research Group
leads.court: Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
leads.text:
1 

United States Court of Appeals 
for the Fifth Circuit 
____________ 

No. 24-40564 
____________ 

United States of America, ex rel, Brook Jackson, 

Plaintiff—Appellant, 

versus 

United States of America, 

Intervenor Plaintiff—Appellee, 

Ventavia Research Group, L.L.C., 

Defendant—Appellee. 
______________________________ 

Appeal from the United States District Court 
for the Eastern District of Texas 
USDC No. 1:21-CV-8 
______________________________ 

Before Elrod, Chief Judge, and Richman and Willett, Circuit Judges. 
Don R. Willett: 
The False Claims Act (FCA)1 deputizes private citizens to litigate on 
the Government’s behalf , but the claims remain the Government’s to 
_____________________ 
1 31 U.S.C. §§ 3729–33. 
United States Court of Appeals 
Fifth Circuit 
FILED 
November 13, 2026 

Thomas B. Plunkett, III 
Clerk 
Case: 24-40564 Document: 120-1 Page: 1 Date Filed: 11/13/2026
No. 24-40564 
2 
control. A relator may bring the suit, but the Government retains the right to 
seek to end it. 
Here, a fter declining to intervene during the seal period, the 
Government moved to intervene and dismiss Brook Jackson ’s lawsuit 
challenging the scientific integrity of Pf izer’s COVID-19 vaccine trials. It 
argued that her claims lacked merit, conflicted with federal public -health 
policy, and would impose heavy litigation and discovery burdens. 
Following the Supreme Court’s guidance in United States ex rel. 
Polansky v. Executive Health Resources, Inc. ,2 we conclude that the district 
court acted well within its discretion in permit ting intervention and 
dismissing Jackson’s FCA claims. The district court also properly dismissed 
Jackson’s separate retaliation claim3 against Ventavia Research Group, LLC 
(Ventavia)—Jackson’s employer and a site operator for Pfizer’s clinical 
trials—for failure to state a claim. 
We therefore AFFIRM the district court’s judgment in full. 
I. Background 
A. The False Claims Act 
The FCA “is the government’s primary litigation tool for recovering 
losses sustained as the result of fraud.” 4 The statute authorizes treble 
damages and civil penalties from persons who knowingly present, or cause to 
be presented, false or fraudulent claims for payment to the G overnment.5 
_____________________ 
2 599 U.S. 419 (2023). 
3 31 U.S.C. § 3730(h). 
4 United States ex rel. Marcy v. Rowan Cos., 520 F.3d 384, 388 (5th Cir. 2008) (citing 
Avco Corp. v. U.S. Dep’t of Just., 884 F.2d 621, 622 (D.C. Cir. 1989)). 
5 31 U.S.C. § 3729(a)(1)(A)–(B). 
Case: 24-40564 Document: 120-1 Page: 2 Date Filed: 11/13/2026
No. 24-40564 
3 
Although the G overnment ordinarily litigates its own claims, the FCA 
contains a qui tam mechanism permitting private relators to file an action “for 
the person and for the United States Government.”6 
Such an action is filed under seal for 60 days —extendable for good 
cause—and served only on the G overnment so it may investigate the 
allegations and decide whether to intervene.7 If the Government declines to 
intervene during the seal period, the relator “shall have the right to conduct 
the action” and proceed on the Government’s behalf.8 Even so, the statute 
allows the Government “to intervene at a later date upon a showing of good 
cause.”9 
Once the Government intervenes—either initially or at a later date—
it obtains “primary responsibility for prosecuting the action,” and the 
relator’s role becomes secondary. 10 Under § 3730(c)(2)(A), “[t]he 
Government may dismiss the action notwithstanding the objections of the 
person initiating the action if the person has been notified by the Government 
of the filing of the motion and the court has provided the person with an 
opportunity for a hearing on the motion .” This language gives the 
Government substantial flexibility. Even after declining to intervene during 
the seal period, the Government may later try to take over and dismiss the 
suit.
11 
_____________________ 
6 Id. § 3730(b)(1). 
7 Id. § 3730(b)(2)–(4). 
8 Id. § 3730(b)(4)(B). 
9 Id. § 3730(c)(3). 
10 Id. § 3730(c)(1). 
11 Polansky, 599 U.S. at 434–38. 
Case: 24-40564 Document: 120-1 Page: 3 Date Filed: 11/13/2026
No. 24-40564 
4 
The FCA also contains a retaliation provision that protects 
whistleblower employees from adverse employment actions for their lawful 
acts “in furtherance of” an FCA lawsuit or “other efforts to stop” FCA 
violations.12 To state a retaliation claim, a plaintiff must plausibly allege that 
(1) she engaged in protected activity, (2) her employer knew of that protected 
activity, and (3) her protected conduct was the cause of the adverse 
employment action.13 
B. Jackson’s Lawsuit 
Ventavia hired Jackson in September 2020 as a regional clinical- trial 
director responsible for vaccine -testing sites, patient recruitment, training, 
and quality assurance. Ventavia operated three clinical trial sites participating 
in Pfizer’s Phase III COVID -19 vaccine trial. As a contract investigator , 
Ventavia’s responsibilities included conducting clinical procedures, 
collecting data, maintaining records, and performing trial-site quality-control 
checks in accordance with Pfizer’s study protocols and FDA Good Clinical 
Practice guidelines. Pfizer also contracted with Icon PLC, a clinical research 
organization, to manage the vaccine trials. 
Jackson began working at Ventavia shortly after Pfizer agreed to 
deliver 100 million doses of an FDA-approved or - authorized COVID-19 
vaccine to the Government. Her tenure lasted roughly two weeks. During 
that time, she developed concerns about protocol deviations and regulatory 
violations. These concerns prompted Jackson to recommend pausing trial 
enrollment while Ventavia addressed the issues and implemented safeguards. 
_____________________ 
12 31 U.S.C. § 3730(h). 
13 United States ex rel. King v. Solvay Pharms., Inc., 871 F.3d 318, 332 (5th Cir. 2017); 
see also United States v. Hodge, 933 F.3d 468, 475 (5th Cir. 2019). 
Case: 24-40564 Document: 120-1 Page: 4 Date Filed: 11/13/2026
No. 24-40564 
5 
Jackson repeatedly reported her concerns to her supervisors during 
her short tenure, and she eventually reported to the FDA her view that the 
trial sites were not operating according to regulatory expectations. The same 
day Jackson contacted the FDA , Ventavia terminated her for not being a 
“good fit .” Ventavia resumed trial enrollment the next day, and Pfizer 
announced favorable results two months later. 
Jackson filed her original complaint under seal in January 2021, 
alleging FCA claims on behalf of the Government against Pfizer, Ventavia, 
and Icon PLC . She also brought a retaliation claim against Ventavia. The 
Government elected not to intervene during the seal period but reserved its 
right to intervene later. After the G overnment declined intervention, the 
district court unsealed Jackson’s complaint, and she proceeded as a qui tam 
relator under § 3730(b)(4)(B). 
Jackson immediately filed her first amended complaint, and all three 
Defendants moved to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6) and Rule 9(b). Although 
the Government did not intervene, it still filed a statement of interest 
supporting dismissal. The district court held a hearing and promptly granted 
the motions. 
Following the dismissal of her claims , Jackson moved for 
reconsideration so that she could amend her complaint to include a 
fraud-in-the-inducement claim. The district court granted her motion. 
Building upon her previous accusations, Jackson’s Second Amended 
Complaint (SAC) alleged, among other things, that Pfizer’s submissions to 
the FDA contained fabricated or manipulated data and excluded reporting 
of serious adverse events. Had the FDA been aware of the alleged 
misconduct, Jackson claimed , the Emergency Use Authorization ( EUA) 
would not have been granted for Pfizer’s vaccine. She further asserted that 
the Government’s subsequent decisions to purchase doses of Pfizer’s 
Case: 24-40564 Document: 120-1 Page: 5 Date Filed: 11/13/2026
No. 24-40564 
6 
vaccine revealed the false claims “caused” by Defendants because the 
underlying data supporting the EUA were purportedly fraudulent. The SAC 
also reasserted a nearly identical retaliation claim against Ventavia that was 
previously dismissed. Defendants again moved to dismiss Jackson’s 
complaint. 
This time, the Government sought to intervene so that it could 
dismiss Jackson’s lawsuit under § 3730(c)(2)(A). In the Government’s view, 
the FCA claims lacked merit, were based on “misinformation,” and were 
inconsistent with public-health policy. The Government also anticipated that 
continued litigation would impose substantial discovery and oversight 
burdens on the FDA, the Department of Health and Human Services 
(HHS), and the Department of Justice ( DOJ). The district court granted 
the Government’s motion, dismissing the FCA claims with prejudice as to 
Jackson and without prejudice as to the Government. 
The district court separately dismissed with prejudice the FCA 
retaliation claim under § 3730(h) against Ventavia for failure to state a claim, 
concluding that Jackson did not sufficiently plead a protected activity or 
Ventavia’s knowledge of this activity . Having dismissed all federal claims, 
the district court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the 
state-law retaliation claim, and denied Jackson leave to amend her complaint 
a third time. 
II. The Government Properly Intervened 
The district court did not abuse its discretion in allowing the 
Government to intervene. 14 The FCA allows intervention after the seal 
_____________________ 
14 See Newby v. Enron Corp., 443 F.3d 416, 423 (5th Cir. 2006). 
Case: 24-40564 Document: 120-1 Page: 6 Date Filed: 11/13/2026
No. 24-40564 
7 
period “upon a showing of good cause.”15 The Government explained that it 
sought dismissal of Jackson’s claims because it believed the suit was unlikely 
to succeed on the merits , would impose substantial discovery and litigation 
burdens, and conflicted with public -health policy. Those reasons readily 
satisfy the statute’s good-cause requirement. 
A. The Governing Standard 
At the outset, the parties disagree about what “good cause” standard 
applies. The Government argues that the district court correctly applied the 
more lenient standard: the articulation of a legally sufficient reason for 
intervention. Jackson, by contrast, argues that the Government was required 
to satisfy Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 24(b) ’s requirements for 
permissive intervention alongside the statute’s good-cause requirement. The 
district court properly held that Rule 24(b) is inapplicable here. 
Section 3730(c)(3) of the FCA does not define “good cause,” and the 
Supreme Court did not expressly evaluate it in Polanksy.16 Even so, the Court

POST-TRIAL MEMORANDUM OPINION 
 
Date Submitted: October 8, 2026 
Date Decided: November 13, 2026 
 
 
Brett M. McCartney, Elizabeth A. Powers, Sarah T. Andrade, BAYARD, P.A., 
Wilmington, DE; Attorneys for Holmwood Capital Advisors, LLC and Holmwood 
Capital, LLC.  
 
S. Michael Sirkin  and R. Garrett Rice, ROSS ARONSTAM & MOR ITZ LLP, 
Wilmington, DE; OF COUNSEL: John T. Floyd  and Kaitlin M. Price, MOORE & 
VAN ALLEN PLLC, Charlotte, NC ; Attorneys for HC Government Realty 
Holdings, L.P. and HC Government Realty Trust, Inc. 
 
 
 
DAVID, V.C. 
1 
 
Four founders formed a series of companies to acquire commercial real estate 
properties subject to long-term leases with federal government tenants.  Among the 
entities, the founders formed a real estate investment trust (“REIT”) to own a holding 
company into which they contributed seven special purpose entities each owning a 
property leased to the government.  They also formed a separate company tha t, for 
a time, provided management services to the REIT and its holding company.  In 
2019, over the objection of some of the founders, the REIT’s board approved a 
recapitalization transaction with a new investor  and terminated the management 
company.  The parties dispute the termination fee the REIT must pay to the 
management company and raise other claims and counterclaims arising from their 
fractured relationship.   
This memorandum opinion follows a three -day trial that centered on the 
proper calculation of the termination fee.  For a reader undeterred by the soporific 
nature of accounting and contractual definitions of stockholders’ equity, the 
selection of securities to pay termination and acquisition fees, public offering 
expense calculations, un-papered loan s, and representations and warranties 
2 
regarding lender consent (among other issues), the five dozen pages that follow are 
sure to delight.1 
I. BACKGROUND 
 The following facts are as the Court finds them following a three -day trial 
held from May 4 through May 6, 2026.2 
A. The Founders Form Holmwood , HCA, HCM, HC REIT , And 
Holdings. 
 In 2010, Edwin M. Stanton, Robert R. Kaplan, Sr. (“Kaplan, Sr.”), Robert R. 
Kaplan, Jr. (“Kaplan, Jr.”), and Dr. Philip Kurlander (together, the “Founders”) 
formed p laintiff Holmwood Capital, LLC (“Holmwood”) , a Delaware limited 
liability company, to acquire commercial real estate properties subject to long-term 
leases with federal government tenants.3 
 In June 2014, the Founders formed a new Delaware limited liability company, 
plaintiff Holmwood Capital Advisors, LLC  (“HCA,” and with Holmwood,

(“SPEs”): GOV Silt, LLC ; GOV Ft. Smith, LLC ; GOV FBI Johnson City, LLC ;

Plaintiff -Appellant, 

v. 

NEWREZ LLC d/b/a 
SHELLPOINT MORTGAGE 
SERVICING,

 Plaintiff -Respondent,

 Defendant -Appellant , 

and 

NOT FOR PUBLICATION WITHOUT THE 
APPROVAL OF THE APPELLATE DIVISION 

This opinion shall not "constitute precedent or be binding upon any court ." Although it is posted on the 
internet , this opinion is binding only on the parties in the case and its use in other cases is limited . R. 1:36 -3. 

2 A-2712 -24 

NEW JERSEY MANUFACTURERS 
INSURANCE , 

 Defendant . 
_____________________ __________ 

Submitted October 28, 2026 – Decided November 1 3, 2026 

Before Judges Mayer and Smith. 

On appeal from the Superior Court of New Jersey, Law 
Division and Chancery Division , Burlington County, 
Docket No s. L-1339-24 and F-003750-23. 

Jonathan Addo, self -represented appellant. 

Husch Blackwell LLP, attorney s for respondent in A-
2712-24 (Laura K. Conroy, of counsel and on the brief). 

Hladik Onorato & Federman, LLP, attorney s for 
respondent in A -2742-24 (Robert W. Williams, on the 
brief). 

PER CURIAM 
 These appeals are calendared back-to-back and consolidated for the 
purpose of issuing a single opinion . The appeal in Docket No. A -2742-24 relates 
to th e foreclosure of real property at 45 Hopewell Lane in Willingboro 
(property) by Newrez LLC d /b/a Shellpoint Mortgage Servicing (Shellpoint) 
(foreclosure action ). The appeal in Docket No. A -2712-24 involves a claim for 
damages by the former property owner, Jonathan Addo, against Shellpoint . We 

3 A-2712 -24 

dismiss the appeal in the foreclosure action and affirm the order s on appeal in 
the Addo action. 
Starting with the foreclosure action, on November 28, 2023, Shellpoint 
obtained a default judgment of foreclosure related to the property . On April 25, 
2024, Shellpoint sold the property at a sheriff 's sale. Six months later, an 
innocent third part y acquired title to the property. 
 On March 18, 2025, well after the sale of the property to the innocent third 
party and sixteen months after entry of the foreclosure judgment, Addo moved 
to set aside the foreclosure judgment and regain possession of the property . He 
argued the foreclosure judgment should be vacated because there was no 
personal jurisdiction, no subject matter jurisdiction, no enforceable lien, and 
Shellpoint violated the New Jersey Court Rules . 
 On April 21, 2025, c iting Rule 4:50-1, the judge denied the motion to 
vacate the foreclosure judgment. The judge found Addo failed to satisfy any of 
the requirements under Rule 4:50 to justify relief from the foreclosure judgment. 
He concluded Addo was "improperly attempting to get another chance to contest 
the validity of the [f]oreclosure [a]ction by asserting a challenge to Shellpoint 's 
standing, which is an essential and 'germane ' claim in [f]oreclosure. " 

4 A-2712 -24 

In June 2024, after the property had been sold at a sheriff 's sale, Addo 
filed an action against Shellpoint (Addo action) . The Addo action asserted the 
following defenses to the foreclosure judgment : (1) "Validation of Debt; 
Accounting "; (2) "Breach of Contract "; (3) "Holder in Due Course "; and (4) 
"Commencement of Foreclosure; Violation of Due Process ." Addo also sought 
damages against Shellpoint based on the alleged improper foreclosure judgment. 
In lieu of filing an answer, Shellpoint moved to dismiss the Addo action . 
It argued Addo improperly sought to relitigate the foreclosure action, and the 
claims in the Addo action w ere precluded by res judicata, collateral estoppel, 
and the entire controversy doctrine. Shellpoint asserted the claims in the Addo 
action regarding standing, the mortgage , and right to due process were germane 
to the foreclosure action and had already been fully adjudicated. 
In opposing dismissal of the Addo action, Addo renewed many of the same 
arguments he previously raised, which the judge rejected in the motion to vacate 
the foreclosure judgment. He further asserted the Addo action was separate and 
distinct from the foreclosure action. 
The judge granted Shellpoint 's motion and dismissed the Addo action with 
prejudice. The judge explained the allegations in the Addo action were "either 
redundant to or issues that should have been and could have been raised in the 

5 A-2712 -24 

context of the foreclosure action. " The judge concluded the Addo action sought 
to "re-litigate " the same issues adjudicated in the foreclosure action and, 
therefore, the claims in the Addo action were barred by res judicata, collateral 
estoppel, and the entire controversy doct rine. 
Addo filed two separate appeals. In Docket No. A-2712-24, Addo 
appealed the order denying his motion to vacate the judgment in the foreclosure 
action. In Docket No. A -2742-24, Addo appeal ed all orders leading to the 
dismissal of the Addo action. 
The Foreclosure Action 
We first address whether Addo's appeal in the foreclosure action should 
be dismissed as moot. "A case is moot if the disputed issue has been resolved, 
at least with respect to the parties who instituted the litigation. " Caput Mortuum 
L.L.C. v. S & S Crown Servs., Ltd. , 366 N.J. Super. 323, 330 (App. Div. 2004) . 
Dismissal is appropriate when "a judgment cannot grant effective relief, or there 
is no concrete adversity of interest between the parties. " Ibid. "An issue is 'moot 
when our decision sought in a matter, when rendered, can have no practical 
effect on the existing controversy. " Redd v. Bowman , 223 N.J. 87, 104 (2015) 
(quoting Deutsch Bank Nat 'l Tr. Co. v. Mitchell , 422 N.J. Super. 214, 221 -22 
(App. Div. 2011) ). 

6 A-2712 -24 

Having reviewed the record, Addo's appeal in t he foreclosure action is 
moot. This court cannot undue the foreclosure acti on because an innocent third 
party now owns the property . Moreover, t his court is unable to grant Addo the 
right to regain the property under the present circumstances . Because this court 
cannot effectively grant relief to Addo, the foreclosure a ction is moot and we 
dismiss that appeal . 
Additionally , w e dismiss Addo 's appeal in the foreclosure action for 
failure to comply with the New Jersey Court Rules. Appellants are required to 
reference the record on appeal . See R. 2:6-8. Further, submission of an 
inadequate appellate brief, requiring the appellate court "independent[ly] 
examin[e] " the record or research the law , violates Rule 2:6-9. 
In both appeals, Addo repeatedly referenced factual assertions without 
support or citation to the record as required by the Court Rules. Addo also 
violated his duty to this court by citing non -existent case law along with cases 
that fail ed to support his legal arguments . Although Addo is a self -represented 
litigant, he is held to the same standard of compliance with the Court Rules as 
an attorney. See Mims v. City of Gloucester , 479 N.J. Super. 1, 4 (App. Div. 
2024). These deficiencies in Addo 's appellate submission s provide an 
alternative basis for dismissal of both appeals . 

7 A-2712 -24 

 Regarding the merits of Addo's appeal in the foreclosure action, we are 
satisfied the judge properly denied the motion to vacate the foreclosure 
judgment as untimely under Rule 4:50-2. Motions to vacate judgment must be 
"made within a reasonable time. " R. 4:50-2. Motions based on Rule 4:50-1(a) 
(mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect), (b) (newly discovered 
evidence), or (c) (fraud, misrepresentation, or other misconduct) impose a strict 
one-year time limit for filing for relief from a judgment . See Romero v. Gold 
Star Distribution , 468 N.J. Super. 274, 296 (App. Div. 2021). 
Here, Addo failed to file the motion to vacate the foreclosure judgment 
until sixteen months after the entry of th at judgment and after the sale of the 
property to an innocent third party purchaser. Addo offers no reasonable 
explanation for the sixteen -month delay in moving to vacate the foreclosure 
judgment. Thus, the judge correctly denied the motion to vacate the foreclosure 
judgment as untimely. 
Additionally, Addo raised arguments for the first time related to his appeal 
in the foreclosure action . His newly asserted arguments were no t presented to 
the trial court. We "decline to consider questions or issues not properly 
presented to the trial court when an opportunity for such a presentation is 
available 'unless the questions raised on appeal go to the jurisdiction of the trial 

8 A-2712 -24 

court or concern matters of great public interest. '" Nieder v. Royal Indem. Ins. 
Co., 62 N.J. 229, 234 (1973) (quoting Reynolds Offset Co., Inc. v. Summer , 58 
N.J. Super. 542, 548 (App. Div. 1959)). Addo 's new arguments do not address 
the trial court 's jurisdiction nor concern matters of significant public interest. 
Thus, we decline to consider Addo's newly asserted arguments on appeal . 
The Addo Action 
 We next consider Addo 's appeal from dismissal of the Addo action. Addo 
argues the judge erred in granting Shellpoint 's dismissal motion based on the 
entire controversy doctrine, res judicata, and collateral estoppel. Addo raises 
the same arguments presented in his appeal from the foreclosure action. 
 We review de novo a trial court 's decision on a motion to dismiss a 
complaint under Rule 4:6-2(e) for failure to state a claim upon which relief may 
be granted. Baskin v. P.C. Richard & Son, LLC , 246 N.J. 157, 171 (2021). On 
review, we examine the motion "by the same standard applied by the trial court; 
thus, considering and accepting as true the facts alleged in the complaint, [and] 
determin[ing] whether they set forth a claim upon which relief can be granted. " 
Sickles v. Cabot Corp. , 379 N.J. Super. 100, 106 (App. Div. 2005) . 
 We review dismissal of an action applying preclusive doctrines such as 
the entire controversy doctrine, res judicata, and collateral estoppel de novo. 

9 A-2712 -24 

Selective Ins. Co. v. McAllister , 327 N.J. Super. 168, 173 (App. Div. 2000). 
After reviewing the record, we are satisfied all three preclusive doctrines barred 
the claims in the Addo action. 
The entire controversy doctrine "embodies the principle that the 
adjudication of a legal controversy should occur in one litigation in only one 
court." Wadeer v. New Jersey Mfrs. Ins. Co. , 220 N.J. 591, 605 (2015) (quoting 
Highland Lakes Country Club & Cmty. Ass 'n v. Nicastro , 201 N.J. 123, 125 
(2009)). Rule 4:30A provides that "[n]on-joinder of claims required to be joined 
by the entire controversy doctrine shall result in the preclusion of the omitted 
claims to the extent required by the entire controversy doctrine. " The entire 
controversy doctrine requires joinder of claims that "'arise from related facts or 
the same transaction or series of transactions ' but need not share common legal 
theories. " Bank Leumi USA v. Kloss , 243 N.J. 218, 226 (2020) (quoting 
Dimitrakopoulos v. Borrus, Goldin, Foley, Vignuolo, Hyman and Stahl, PC , 237 
N.J. 91, 1 19 (2019)). "The doctrine may be applied even against a party which 
defaults in the first proceeding. " Joan Ryno, Inc. v. First Nat. Bank of S. Jersey , 
208 N.J. Super. 562, 569 (App. Div. 1986) (citing Mori v. Hartz Mountain 
Development Corp. , 193 N.J. Super. 47, 55 -56 (App. Div. 1983)). 

10 A-2712 -24 

"Res judicata, like the entire controversy doctrine, serves the purpose of 
providing 'finality and repose; prevention of needless litigation; avoidance of 
duplication; reduction of unnecessary burdens of time and expenses; elimination 
of conflicts, confusion and uncertainty; and basic fairness[.] '" Wadeer, 220 N.J. 
at 606 (alterations in original) (quoting First Union Nat 'l Bank v. Penn Salem 
Marina, Inc. , 190 N.J. 342, 352 (2007) (internal quot

Huntsville Design and Construction, Inc.  
 
v.  
 
Linda Morard and Oliver Augustus Morard III 
 
 Appeal from Madison Circuit Court 
(CV-25-900587) 
 
WISE, Justice. 
 
 Huntsville Design and Construction , Inc. ("HDC"), appeals from the 
Madison Circuit Court's judgment di smissing its claims against Linda 
SC-2026-0120 
2 
 
Morard ("Linda") and Oliver Augustus Morard III ("Oliver").  We dismiss 
the appeal. 
Facts and Procedural History 
 On April 8, 2025, HDC sued Linda, Oliver, CAM, LLC ("CAM"), 
David P. Bristol, and Acquisition In tegration, LLC ("AI"), in the trial 
court.  In its complaint HDC allege d that Linda, Oliver, and/or CAM 
(collectively referred to as "the CAM defendants") owned property located 
on 146 Jim Harding Way in Huntsvil le ("the subject property").  HDC 
further alleged that, on or about Au gust 31, 2022, it entered into a 
contract with the CAM defendants "to construct a structure at" the 
subject property ("the CAM contract").   
HDC further alleged that, on or about December 9, 2022, it entered 
into a contract with Bristol and AI (collectively referred to as "the AI 
defendants") "to construct a structur e at" the subject property, which, 
HDC asserted, the AI defendants "intended on purchasing"; HDC's 
contract with the AI defendants is referred to as "the AI contract."  HDC 
alleged that, "at all times, it acted in accord with the contract terms 
established by the parties, in reference to the aforementioned contracts" 
and that it had completed the terms of the contracts.   
SC-2026-0120 
3 
 
HDC further alleged that the AI  defendants did not complete 
payments to HDC; that, as of October 31, 2023, the AI defendants owed 
an outstanding balance of $305,019 to HDC; that Bristol had sent text 
messages in which he stated that  he would issue payment to HDC 
immediately; that, on January 26, 2025, Bristol wrote a check on AI's 
account for the amount owed, but that  check was returned by the bank 
for insufficient funds; and that HDC had made numerous attempts to 
collect the outstanding balance.  HDC further alleged: 
"That prior to contracting with [Bristol] and [AI] on December 
9, 2022, [HDC] expressed conc erns about contracting with 
[Bristol] and [AI] to [Linda], due to not having done business 
with them before.  [Linda] resp onded by stating that, if [AI] 
did not pay [HDC] under its contract, that [Linda] would pay 
what was due under the AI Contract, thereby inducing [HDC] 
to enter the AI Contract." 
 
HDC alleged that, on July 18, 2024,   it "filed a Mechanic's Lien 
against the [subject] property" in the Madison Probate Court; that, 
"[t]hereafter, Linda, Oliver, and/or CAM, as the property owners, sold the 
[subject] property"; that, on Decemb er 26, 2024, Linda made the final 
payment under the CAM contract; an d that the CAM defendants failed 
or refused to pay the outstanding balance owed to HDC under the AI 
contract.  It further alleged "[t]hat the Defendants intentionally and/or 
SC-2026-0120 
4 
 
recklessly accepted the Plaintiff's co nstruction work, without intending 
to pay the entire contract costs."   
 HDC alleged a claim of "breach of  implied/express contract" against 
Linda.  In that claim, HDC alleged that, before HDC entered into the  AI 
contract, Linda had "promised to pa y any outstanding amounts owed to 
[HDC] under the AI contract, if [Bristol] and/or [AI] did not pay [HDC]," 
and that Linda had failed to pay the outstanding amounts that were owed 
to HDC under the AI contract.  HDC al so asserted claims of fraudulent 
misrepresentation and/or innocent misrepresentation against CAM and 
Linda.  With regard to the misr epresentation claim against CAM, HDC 
alleged that, before it entered into the AI contract, Linda "on behalf of 
[CAM], asked [HDC] to contract with [AI] and [Bristol] to build out the 
building owned by [CAM] and/or [Linda] located at [the subject property] 
and[,] in exchange for [HDC's] doing so, promised to pay any outstanding 
amounts owed to [HDC] under the AI contract if [Bristol] and/or [AI] did 
not pay [HDC]."  It also alleged: 
"51. That, throughout this process, Linda Morard, 
individually and on behalf of   [CAM] represented that she 
fully intended to pay the amounts owed to [HDC] for the work 
performed at said property und er the AI Contract.  [HDC] 
believed these representations, given the assurances asserted 
by [Linda] and [CAM] and due to  their repetitive business 
SC-2026-0120 
5 
 
relationship, to its detriment.  [Linda] individually and on 
behalf of [CAM] made these representations recklessly and/or 
intentionally to secure  cons truction and im provement work 
by [HDC] while intending to not comply with the contract 
terms agreed to by the parties." 
 
With regard to the misrepresentation claim against Linda, the 
complaint alleged that, before HDC en tered into the AI contract, Linda 
had "promised to pay any outstanding amounts owed to [HDC] under the 
AI contract if [Bristol] and/or [AI] did not pay [HDC]."  It further alleged: 
"59. That, throughout this process, [Linda] represented 
that she fully intended to pay the amounts owed to [HDC] for 
the work performed at said property, including any 
outstanding amounts owed under the AI Contract.  [HDC] 
believed these representations, given the relationship 
between [HDC] and [Linda], to its detriment.  [Linda] made 
these representations reckless ly and/or intentionally to 
secure construction and impr ovement work by [HDC] while 
intending to not comply with th e contract terms agreed to by 
the parties. 
 
"60. Further, the represen tations made by [Linda] 
regarding her promise to pay any outstanding amounts owed 
under the AI Contract if [Bristol] and/or AI did not pay [HDC] 
fraudulent [sic] induced [HDC] to enter into the December 9, 
2022, contract with said Defendants, to [HDC's] detriment. 
 
"…. 
 
"62. That throughout this process, [Linda], individually 
and on behalf of [CAM], represented that she fully intended 
to pay the amounts owed to [HDC] for the work performed at 
said property under the AI Co ntract.  [HDC] believed these 
representations, given the assu rances asserted by [Linda], 
SC-2026-0120 
6 
 
and due to their repetitive business relationship, to its 
detriment.  [Linda] made thes e representations recklessly 
and/or intentionally to secure construction and improvement 
work by [HDC] while intendin g to not comply with the 
contract terms agreed to by the parties." 
 
HDC also asserted a bad-faith clai m against Linda in which it again 
alleged that, before it entered into the AI contract, Linda had agreed to 
pay any outstanding balances owed to HDC under the AI contract in the 
event that Bristol and/or AI did not pay.   
HDC also asserted an unjust-enrichment claim against each of the 
CAM defendants in which it alleged that it had provided the CAM 
defendants "with something of valu e, i.e., construction improvement 
services," and that the CAM defendants had "acknowledged, accepted 
and benefitted from the services and improvements provided to [them] 
by [HDC], and [have] further pr ofited from said services and 
improvements through the sale of  [the subject pr operty] without 
providing payment of the outstand ing amounts to" HDC.  HDC also 
asserted a quantum meruit claim an d a suppression claim against each 
of the CAM defendants.  Finally, HD C asserted claims of breach of 
implied/express contract, fraudulent misrepresentation and/or innocent 
SC-2026-0120 
7 
 
misrepresentation, bad faith, unjust  enrichment, quantum meruit, and 
suppression against the AI defendants.1 
 On May 14, 2025, the CAM defend ants filed a motion to dismiss 
pursuant to Rule 12(b)(6), Ala. R. Civ. P.  In their motion, the CAM 
defendants argued that HDC's claims  against them were barred by the 
Statute of Frauds because the alleged promise to pay the debts of the AI 
defendants was not in writing. 
 On May 16, 2025, the trial co urt entered an order stating: 
"The Court has received the MOTION TO DISMISS, 
filed on behalf of  Defendants Linda Morard, Oliver A. Morard 
III and CAM, LLC, and has considered the grounds and 
determines the Statute of Frauds is applicable to their claims.  
[HDC] shall produce for the Co urt within five days any 
writing by Linda Morard, or an authorized representative of 
CAM, LLC, wherein they promis e to cover the outstanding 
debt of David P. Bristol or AI ….   
 
"In the event that no such writing is produced or exists, 
the case against those specific Defendants will be dismissed." 
 
 On May 19, 2025, HDC filed a moti on for an extension of time to 
respond to the trial court's May 16, 2025, order.  In that motion, plaintiff's 
counsel stated, in part: 
 
1On May 21, 2025, the trial court entered a default judgment in 
favor of HDC and against Bristol.

8 
 
 "The undersigned believes there may be a writing in 
existence that will directly sati sfy the Defendants' Statute of 
Frauds argument.  Additi onally, the undersigned 
understands Defendants' argument; however, it is believed 
that this issue will be fall [sic ] under one of the exceptions to 
the Statute of Frauds requirements.  Prior to the 
undersigned's illness, the undersigned had located case 
precedent which appears to have  directly contradicted the 
Defendants' Statute of Frauds argument.  [HDC] would 
request that [it] be provided an opportunity, via Response and 
Hearing, to present this argument to this Honorable Court." 
 
The trial court granted HDC's motion for an extension of time.   
On May 28, 2025, HDC filed a motion to alter, amend, or vacate the 
trial court's May 16, 2025, order requiring the produc tion of a writing.  
The CAM defendants filed a response in opposition to HDC's motion to 
alter, amend, or vacate.  The trial court entered an order denying CAM's 
motion to alter, amend, or vacate.  However, it set a hearing on the CAM 
defendants' motion to dismiss.  In th at order, the trial court stated, in 
part: "Thirty minutes is allotted for the hearing and the signed writing, 
wherein Defendant Linda Morard obligates herself to [HDC], must be 
produced, or the case against her will be DISMISSED."  (Emphasis in 
original.)   
On June 4, 2025, HDC filed its re sponse to the CAM defendants' 
motion to dismiss.  In its response, HDC argued  that Linda's promise to 
SC-2026-0120 
9 
 
pay was "an original agreement" that  was not within the Statute of 
Frauds.  On June 5, 2025, the tria l court conducted a hearing on the 
m o t i o n  t o  d i s m i s s .    D u r i n g  t h e  h e a ring, the trial court stated that it 
would take the matter under advisement. 
On June 11, 2025, the trial court entered an order in which it stayed 
its ruling on the motion to dismis s "until September 12, 2025, when a 
hearing will be held at 9:00 a.m."  It further ordered the parties to proceed 
with discovery.  Finally, the trial court stated:  "Based upon the pleadings 
of the parties thus far, the Court still believes that the Statute of Fraud[s] 
applies to collateral promises by a third party to pay for the debt of 
another."  The trial court subsequently continued the hearing to October 
30, 2025.

Rel: November 13, 2026 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Notice: This opinion is subject to formal revision before publication in the advance sheets of Southern

300 Dexter Avenue, Montgomery, Alabama 36104-3741 ((334) 229-0650), of any typographical or other 
errors, in order that corrections may be made before the opinion is printed in Southern Reporter. 
 
 
SUPREME COURT OF ALABAMA 
 
OCTOBER TERM, 2026-2027 
 
_________________________ 
 
SC-2025-0840 
_________________________ 
 
Norfolk Southern Corporation et al.  
 
v.  
 
Bellsouth Telecommunications, LLC, d/b/a AT&T Alabama  
 
(Certified Question from the United States District Court for 
the Northern District of Alabama, Southern Division: 2:25-cv-
00375-GMB) 
 
 
PER CURIAM. 
  
 
SC-2025-0840 
2 
 
Earlier this year, this Court agreed  to answer a question certified 
to us from the United States District  Court for the Northern District of 
Alabama concerning the installation of telecommunications equipment 
at railroad crossings: 
"In Alabama, does a tele communications provider 
installing any kind of telecommunications facilities within the 
margin of the right-of-way of a public roadway have an 
unqualified right to cross a ra il corridor without the 
permission of the railroad?" 
 
Today, after careful consideration and deliberation, we exercise our 
discretion to decline to answer this question. 
 QUESTION DECLINED. 
 Stewart, C.J., and Shaw, Brya n, Sellers, Mendheim, Cook, and 
McCool, JJ., concur.  
Parker, J., concurs specially, with opinion.  
Wise, J., recuses herself. 
 
SC-2025-0840 
3 
 
PARKER, Justice (concurring specially). 
 I concur with our decision not to  answer the certified question. The 
certified-question procedure is a vita l aspect of our federal system. And 
the current question points to stat e-law issues that are important and 
unsettled. But after due consideration, I have concluded that now is not 
the right time to try to resolve them.  
I. 
A great deal of litigation in this State occurs in federal courts, and 
those federal courts must frequently apply Alabama law. But this Court 
remains the final arbiter on all ma tters of Alabama law. See Arizonans 
for Official English v. Arizona, 520 U.S. 43, 75-80 (1997).  
Recognizing this tension, the certified-question procedure 
establishes a system of "cooperative federalism." Berkley Reg'l Ins. Co. v. 
Doe Battery Manufacturer, 173 F.4th 989, 993 (8th Cir. 2026). Under this 
procedure, our Court may give clear guidance to the federal courts on 
unsettled matters of Alabama law -- at least when doing so will prove 
"determinative" of a particular case pending in federal court. Ala. R. App. 
P. 18(a). This procedure allows our Court to answer questions of Alabama 
law rather than simply leaving the fe deral courts to guess at what we 
SC-2025-0840 
4 
 
might say. See Berkley Reg'l, 173 F.4th at 992. For all its costs and delay, 
the certified-question procedure is also more efficient than another 
alternative -- federal-court abstention (that is, a stay of the federal case) 
in favor of a "full round of litigation in the state court system before any 
resumption of proceedings in fede ral court." Arizonans for Official 
English, 520 U.S. at 76. 
 The Alabama Constitution expressl y grants this Court "original 
jurisdiction" to "answer questions of state law certified by a court of the 
United States." Ala. Const. 2022, Art. VI, § 140(b). And ordinarily, "[w]e 
have no more right to decline the exer cise of jurisdiction which is given, 
than to usurp that which is not give n." Cohens v. Virginia, 19 U.S. 264, 
404 (1821). But it should also go without saying that we cannot and 
should not answer every conceivable state-law question that might arise 
during federal litigation. This, pres umably, is why the federal courts 
have acknowledged our broad discre tion in deciding how, and even 
whether, to answer a certified question. See, e.g., Alabama State Conf. of 
NAACP v. Attorney General of Alabama, 161 F.4th 1286, 1300 (11th Cir. 
2025).  
SC-2025-0840 
5 
 
The question thus becomes: "What considerations should justify us 
in not answering a certified question?" Without attempting to exhaust all 
possible answers to that question, I can think of at least a few: 
 The question should be determin ative. Our appellate rules say 
that the answer to any ce rtified question must be 
"determinative" of the federal litigation. Ala. R. App. P. 18(a); see 
also New York Times Co. v. Spears, [Ms. SC-2025-0370, Apr. 10, 
2026] ___ So. 3d ___ (Ala. 2026) (declining to answer a certified 
question after initial acceptance  because it proved not to be 
determinative).   
 The question should relate to an unsettled area. Our appellate 
rules also say that there mu st be "no clear controlling 
precedents" from this Court. Ala. R. App. P. 18(a). 
 The question should be important. Any certified question should 
likely be one of "widespread [public] importance." Berkley Reg'l, 
173 F.4th at 992.  
 The question should be purely legal. A certified question should 
ideally be "purely legal" in natu re -- in other words, cleanly 
presented and capable of clean resolution through traditional 
legal reasoning. Executive Plaz a, LLC v. Peerless Ins. Co., 717 
F.3d 114, 118 (2d Cir. 2013). A "clean" question can still turn on 
facts, but the facts should be sufficiently developed to permit an 
informed answer, capable of ready determination. 
By working through these (and perhaps other) considerations, we, and 
the federal courts themselves, can be sure that any certified question is 
truly capable of being answered -- an d that any answer we provide will 
truly matter. 
SC-2025-0840 
6 
 
 This case presents difficulties related to the first and last of the 
above considerations. The federal district court in this case certified this 
question of Alabama law following the filing of a motion for a preliminary 
injunction. But at that point, there had been li ttle factual development, 
and the issues had not been narrow ed or sharpened by the ordinary 
course of litigation. Cf. Stewart Title Guar. Co. v. Shelby Realty Holdings, 
LLC, 83 So. 3d 469 (2011) (declining to  answer a certified question after 
initially consenting). As further expl ained, this circumstance makes it 
unclear whether the question is a pu rely legal one -- and, relatedly, 
whether our answer would truly be determinative. 
II. 
 The parties' dispute centers on an Alabama statute that grants a 
right-of-way to certain people and corporations to construct "electric 
transmission, telegraph, or telephon e lines … along the margin of the 
right-of-way of public highways." Ala. Code 1975, § 23-1-85. The dispute 
certainly entails a question of stat utory interpretation. But it also 
includes an antecedent question about property rights. Difficulties arise 
in answering both of these questions.  
 
SC-2025-0840 
7 
 
A. 
 Because the right-of-way statute essentially conveys an easement, 
it can convey only those property rights already held by the government 
in the public-highway ri ght-of-way. After all, "one cannot convey more 
property than one owns." Hinote v.  Owens, 248 So. 3d 964, 967 (Ala. 
2017). So, before AT&T can build anything in reliance on the right-of-way 
statute, we must first ask whether the government could build the same 
thing without exceeding the government's own right-of-way.  
My research suggests that the answer to this question may vary by 
location. In general, the government  has broad rights to control the 
public-highway right-of-way. See, e.g., Crawford v. Alabama Power Co., 
221 Ala. 236, 238-39, 128 So. 454, 457-58 (1930). And, in general, railroad 
companies have broad rights to cont rol the railroad right-of-way. See, 
e.g., Central of Georgia Ry. Co. v. Faulkner, 217 Ala. 82, 84, 114 So. 686, 
687 (Ala. 1927). But where public roads and railroads intersect, it 
appears that a new use may interf ere with a preexisting use only 
sparingly. Specifically, the new use may be permissible if (1) "it can be 
done without destroying the use of the original way" and (2) it 
"interfere[s] as little as possible with the original use." Southern Ry. Co. 
SC-2025-0840 
8 
 
v. Todd, 279 Ala. 260, 263, 184 So. 2d 341, 344 (1966); see also Ala. Code 
1975, § 18-1A-72.  
On my reading of the law, then, th e scope of a right-of-way is fact-
intensive and dependent upon the manner in which the right-of-way 
arose. See Western Ry. of Alabama v. Alabama Grand Trunk R.R., 96 
Ala. 272, 277-79, 11 So. 483, 485 (1892) (discussing differences between 
express dedication, condemnation, and prescription). But therein lies the 
rub for purposes of our certified-ques tion procedure: This fact-intensive 
and location-specific nature of the i ssue makes it virtually impossible to 
fashion any general answer to the certified question. For this same 
reason, it is also difficult to see how we can arrive at a statement of the 
law that in any respect would be "determinative" of the federal dispute. 
B. 
 Related problems arise in interp reting the right-of-way statute. 
Here, the overarching question boils down to whether fiber-optic cables 
fall within the statute's reference to "electric transmission, telegraph, or 
telephone lines." § 23-1-85. Although  the parties did not raise the 
question before the district court, th e district court's certification order 
pointed out that the answer is at least not obvious. Deciding how to 
SC-2025-0840 
9 
 
interpret statutory language over a ce ntury old in light of technological 
developments can pose both legal and factual difficulties.  
Some of the legal questions includ e: How general is a word like 
"telephone?" What about when it is pa ired with "line?" What do we do 
with the history of statutory amen dments given that "telegraph" was 
added to the right-of-way statute in 1855, 1 "telephone" was added in 
1897,2 and "electric transmission" was added in 1975? 3 How broadly or 
narrowly should such terms be read when faced with technology not in 
existence at the time? At what leve l of generality should we understand 
the original public meaning of such  terms? What other statutes can 
inform our understanding of this one? 
Factual questions include issues of how the relevant technology 
works: What, exactly, do fiber-optic cables do? To what extent do they 
facilitate telephone service? And how ha s fiber-optic cables' relationship 
to telephone service changed over time? Similarly, are there factual 
differences in telegraph and teleph one technology that might explain 
 
1 See Ala. Acts 1855-1856, Act No. 6. 
 
2 See Ala. Code 1897, § 2490. 
 
3 See Ala. Code 1975, § 23-1-85. 
SC-2025-0840 
10 
 
why the Legislature presumably concluded that the word "telegraph" did 
not include telephone lines and t hus necessitated the addition of 
"telephone" in 1897? 
Having answers to these questions would be helpful if not essential 
to a proper interpretation of the ri ght-of-way statute. Their existence 
underscores why the questi on is not sufficiently "c lean" as to permit us 
to answer the question. 
III. 
 Today's nonanswer to the certified question may be frustrating, but 
a job worth doing is a job worth doing right. Perhaps there will be another 
occasion to consider this questi on -- perhaps with a more narrowed 
question and more developed argume nts and record. In the meantime, I 
remain fully committed to answering certified questions when feasible 
and appropriate. I only reluctantl y conclude that the circumstances 
prevent us from providing such an answer at this time.
