SUPREME COURT OF ALABAMA 

OCTOBER TERM, 2026-2027 

_________________________ 

SC-2026-0206 
_________________________ 

William D. Carpenter 

v. 

Shirley H. Jacobs; Tracey E. Martin; Sharon Baber Turner; 
Marjory Klusman; Leonard W. Mikkelsen; Frank Roberts, Jr.; 
Wide Open Enterprises, LLC; Yvette H. Jones; Victoria Lynn 
Dumas Turner; Lorenzo Evans, Jr.; Ramona Evans; Edward R. 
Slaughter, Jr.; Frances A. Jones; Deborah Ann Gollotte Mabry; 
Donna Leanne Gollotte; Belinda Faye Gollotte Armour; Annis 
McGraw; Janine E. Wallace; Estate of Betty Smith Lott, 
deceased; Janet Lyn Graves; Bradford R. Graves; and Myrtle F. 
Smith 

 Appeal from Mobile Circuit Court 
(CV-24-902172) 
SC-2026-0206 
2 

COOK, Justice. 
William D. Carpenter alleges that, since 2018, stormwater runoff 
from adjoining properties in th e Crown Pointe subdivision ("the 
subdivision") has been flowing onto his property and causing damage. In 
2020, Carpenter sued the Crown Pointe Owners' Association, Inc. ("the 
CPOA"), and the four owners of the properties within the subdivision that 
are nearest his property, asserting va rious tort claims arising from the 
alleged runoff. 
In April 2022, Carpenter obtain ed a jury verdict for $200,000, 
resulting in a judgment against the CPOA. Before that case proceeded to 
trial, Carpenter had entered in to written pro tanto settlement 
agreements containing releases with three of the lot owners -- Janine E. 
Wallace ("Wallace"), Betty Smith Lo tt ("Lott"), and Myrtle F. Smith 
("Smith").1 

1The fourth adjoining lot owner, Bradford R. Graves, received a 
final judgment in his favor. 

The trial court reduced the $200,000 jury verdict for the cumulative 
amounts from the pro tanto settlemen t agreements so that the final 
judgment against the CPOA was for $126,504.64, including costs. 
SC-2026-0206 
3 

According to Carpenter, the drainage problems continued after the 
entry of the 2022 judgment. Carpente r also experienced problems in 
collecting the 2022 judgment. In re sponse, in August 2024, Carpenter 
commenced the present action in the Mobile Circuit Court against (1) the 
CPOA; (2) the individual owners and residents of each of the subdivision's 
lots ("the 21 Lot Owners");2 (3) a newly created homeowners' association, 
Crown Pointe West Homeowners' Asso ciation, Inc. ("the CPWHA"), and 
(4) fictitiously named defendants. In his complaint, Carpenter also styled 
certain claims against "the CPOA Board" and "the CPWHA Board," but 
those terms are simply shorthand for the six individuals who served on 
one or both of those bo ards. Each of those six board members owns or 
resides on a lot and is thus also one of the 21 Lot Owners. The 21 Lot 
Owners therefore consists of the si x board members and the remaining 
lot owners, who did not serve on either board ("the non-board-member lot 

2We note that the term "the 21 Lo t Owners" comes directly from 
Carpenter's second amended complaint and refers to the fact that there 
are 21 lots in the subdivision. It is not meant to imply that there are only 
21 individual lot-owner defendants; some lots have multiple owners. This 
defendant group is composed of lo t owners who served on the CPOA 
Board and/or the CPWHA Board as well as non-board-member lot 
owners. 

SC-2026-0206 
4 

owners"). In the present action, Carp enter alleges claims related to the 
continued discharge of stormwater ru noff onto his property and claims 
related to the defendants' alleged efforts to avoid paying the earlier 2022 
judgment. 
After some procedural back and forth, and the filing of a second 
amended complaint, most of the 21 Lot Owners sought dismissal of the 
claims against them under Rule 12(b)(6), Ala. R. Civ. P. 3 As explained 
below, the chief claim against the 21 lot owners is that they allegedly own 
an undivided interest in a common area that is draining onto Carpenter's 
property. Those defendants dispute th e claim of ownership. They argue 
that the CPOA instead owns the drai nage easement at issue and that, 
even if they owned an undivided inte rest in this property, there are no 
allegations that they have done anything to create this alleged drainage 
problem. Among the 21 Lot Owner s are Wallace and Smith, who 

3Nearly all the 21 Lot Owners joined the motion to dismiss filed by 
Marjory Klusman apart from Edward R. Slaughter, Jr., and Frances A. 
Jones (the owners of Lot 15) and Mary Roberts (a CPOA board member 
and resident of Lot 7). The former two defendants filed their own separate 
motions while the latter, Mary Roberts, according to the record, did not 
file a motion to dismiss despite the fac t that the other resident of Lot 7, 
Frank Roberts, Jr., did so. 
SC-2026-0206 
5 

additionally argue that their writte n pro tanto settlement agreements 
should be enforced and thus bar any further claims against them. 
The circuit court eventually gran ted both the motion to dismiss 
Carpenter's claims against the non-board-member lot owners (see note 3, 
supra) and the motion to enforce Wallace and Smith's settlement 
agreements. Although claims against the CPOA and the six board 
members -- including the claims asserted against those board members 
as lot owners -- remain pending, the circuit court certified its orders as 
final pursuant to Rule 54(b), Ala. R. Civ. P. 
Carpenter now appeals, arguing th at the circuit court erred in 
dismissing his claims against the no n-board-member lot owners and in 
enforcing Wallace's and Smith's settl ement agreements. Before we may 
consider the merit of those arguments, however, we must first determine 
whether the circuit court properly cert ified its dismissal orders as final 
under Rule 54(b). For the reasons set fo rth below, we conclude that the 
Rule 54(b) certification was improper an d, therefore, that this appeal is 
due to be dismissed. 
Facts and Procedural History 
I. The Subdivision 
SC-2026-0206 
6 

The subdivision is a 21-lot resi dential development in Mobile 
County that is subject to a recorded declaration of covenants, conditions, 
restrictions, and easements ("the Decl aration"). Every lot owner in the 
subdivision is a member of the CP OA. The Declaration provides that 
"[e]ach conveyance of Lots 1 thro ugh and including 21 of the herein 
described Property shall also includ e for each such Lot an undivided 
1/21st interest in and to the Common Property subject to the provisions 
hereinafter contained." The map of th e recorded plat depicts a 10-foot 
"drainage and utility easement" adjacent to and south of Lots 18 through 
21 ("the drainage easement"). Ca rpenter alleges that, since 2018, 
stormwater has flowed downhill from the drainage easement behind lots 
18 through 21 and has damaged his property. 
II. Carpenter's 2020 Action and the Pro Tanto Releases 

In July 2020, Carpenter filed suit against the CPOA, Wallace, Lott, 
Smith, and Bradford R. Graves (see note 1, supra) in the Mobile Circuit 
Court.4 In his complaint, Carpenter alleged claims of negligence, 

4Wallace (Lot 18), Lott (Lot 19), Graves (Lot 20), and Smith (Lot 21) 
were named in the 2020 action because of their ownership of the lots in 
the subdivision closest to Carpenter's property. 

SC-2026-0206 
7 

wantonness, trespass, nuisance, and "negligent channelization" arising 
from the stormwater runoff onto his property ("the 2020 action"). 
Before trial, Carpenter entered into pro tanto settlements with 
Wallace, Lott, and Smith. The releas e Carpenter executed in favor of 
Wallace on March 5, 2021, provided, in part: 
"In keeping with the foregoing, this Pro Tanto Release shall 
preclude any actions or claims for any future water intrusions 
or other water related claims against Releasees unless such 
claims arise from material changes made to Releasee's 
property after the execution of this document." 

The release Carpenter executed in favor of Smith on April 3, 2022, 
provided, in part: 
"This Pro Tanto Release shall pr eclude any actions or claims 
by … Carpenter (or those succeeding to the rights of 
Carpenter) against Myrtle Smit h for future water intrusions 
alleged to occur on Carpenter' s property unless such claims 
arise from a material change to the drainage on or from 
Myrtle Smith's property. Exampl es of a material change or 
material changes to Myrtle Smith's property would be 
removing or altering the existi ng berm; altering changing or 
adding underground piping; installing additional gutters 
and/or down spouts; and/or taking any other action that would 
materially change or alter the presently existing stormwater 
drainage on Myrtle Smith's property." 

The claims against Wallace and Smith in the 2020 action were dismissed 
with prejudice. 
SC-2026-0206 
8 

On April 7, 2022, a jury returned a $200,000 verdict in Carpenter's 
favor against the CPOA. That verdict was reduced by the $84,000 paid in 
the pro tanto settlements, and Carpenter recorded a judgment against 
the CPOA for $126,504.64, including costs ("the 2022 judgment"). 
III. Events After the Entry of the 2022 Judgment 
Carpenter alleges that, after the entry of the 2022 judgment, the 
CPOA Board took steps to keep him from collecting it. In early August 
2022, Carpenter garnished the CPOA 's bank account for $1,516.18. 
Carpenter alleges that, on August 26, 2022, the CPOA Board opened a 
checking account in the names of board members Barbara W. Cain and 
Mary M. Roberts and directed the lot owners to pay their dues and 
assessments to Cain or Roberts rather than to the CPOA. The CPOA filed 
a Chapter 7 bankruptcy petition on June 9, 2023. In August 2023, the 
CPOA Board voted to form the CPWH A, and the lot owners were later 
instructed to pay their dues to the CPWHA. The bankruptcy court 
dismissed the CPOA's petition for cause on July 23, 2024. 
During the same period, the CPOA arranged for drainage work 
behind Lots 18 through 21. The minut es of an August 18, 2022, special 
meeting of the CPOA Board state: 
SC-2026-0206 
9 

"We are still going to have to fix the problem of water 
onto Mr. Carpenter's property. Wade Jones, Brad Graves and 
Barbara Cain met with Daniel Le ggett to get an estimate of 
the fix. Have not received a bid from him yet." 

On September 19, 2022, The Ground s Guys submitted a proposal 
addressed to "Crown Pointe HOA" fo r "[d]rainage for behind the first 4 
houses." In November 2022, the CPOA levied a special assessment on the 
owners of each of the subdivision's 21 lots that included $11,119.59 for 
The Grounds Guys. According to Carpenter, The Grounds Guys 
performed the work in March 2023. 
IV. The Present Action 
On August 21, 2024, Carpenter co mmenced this action against the 
CPOA, the CPWHA, and the owners of the subdivision's 21 lots in the 
Mobile Circuit Court. Certain counts are styled as allegations against 
"the CPOA Board" and/or "the CPWHA Board." In his operative pleading, 
the second amended complaint file d on August 25, 2025, Carpenter 
defines "the CPOA Board" as six individuals: Wade L. Jones, Barbara W. 
Cain, Mary E. Jackson, Diane Mikkel sen, Janice Gollotte, and Mary M. 
Roberts; and defines "the CPWHA Boar d" as the same group, with the 
exception of Roberts. Because ever y member of the CPWHA Board also 
served on the CPOA Board, we refer to these individuals in our discussion 
SC-2026-0206 
10 

as "the six board members" even th ough Roberts served only on the 
CPOA Board. 
The second amended complaint refe rs to the defendants that are 
owners and residents of each lot as "the 21 Lot Owners."5 Each of the six

leads.caseName: Pharming Capital, LLC v. James R. Turner
leads.text:
Rel: November 13, 2026 

Notice: This opinion is subject to formal revision before publication in the advance sheets of Southern 
Reporter. Readers are requested to notify the Reporter of Decisions, Alabama Appellate Courts, 
300 Dexter Avenue, Montgomery, Alabama 36104-3741 ((334) 229-0650), of any typographical or other 
errors, in order that corrections may be made before the opinion is printed in Southern Reporter. 

SUPREME COURT OF ALABAMA 

OCTOBER TERM, 2026-2027 

_________________________ 

SC-2025-0453 
_________________________ 

Pharming Capital, LLC 

v. 

James R. Turner 

 Appeal from Coffee Circuit Court 
(CV-24-900062) 

WISE, Justice. 

Pharming Capital, LLC, appeals from a judgment the Coffee Circuit 
Court entered in favor of James R. Tu rner. We reverse the trial court's 
SC-2025-0453 
2 

judgment and remand this case for proceedings consistent with this 
opinion. 
Facts and Procedural History 
This case arises from a rent-to-own contract for a portable building. 
Pharming Capital is a rental compan y that would often purchase such 
contracts through a settlement process, and Blue House Rentals ("BHR") 
would manage those contracts for Pharming Capital. 
On November 21, 2023, Leland Hedlund entered into a rent-to-own 
contract for a "Premier Lofted Barn Cabin" ("the building" or "the cabin"). 
Premier Portable Buildings ("PPB") in Marianna, Florida was the dealer 
who leased the building to Hedlun d. Hedlund executed a "Work 
Order/Contract" ("the work order"). On the work order, the "OWN" box 
was checked with regard to the land where the building would be placed. 
The customer address section in the work order listed "Customer will 
call" for Hedlund's street address, bu t it indicated it was in Bellwood, 
Florida. With regard to the delivery address, it indicated "Customer will 
call" in the section for the street address, but indicated that the delivery 
address was in Bellwood, Alabama. Hedlund also executed a "Rental-
Purchase Agreement and Disclosu re Statement -- Alabama" ("the 
SC-2025-0453 
3 

agreement"), which indicated that BHR Management, LLC, was the 
lessor. The address listed in the ag reement also stated "Customer will 
call" for Hedlund's street address, but the agreement indicated the 
address was located in Bellwood, Florida. The agreement did not include 
any information in the section regard ing the legal owner or landlord of 
the property where the building was to be placed. Additionally, the 
agreement indicated that BHR Manage ment assigned its rights under 
the agreement to Pharming Capital on that same date. However, 
evidence was also presented that the building was a used cabin that 
Pharming Capital owned, that there was no process or settlement in this 
case, and that this "was just a commi ssion sale and deliver price." In 
December 2023, PPB delivered the build ing to land located in Bellwood, 
Alabama, in Geneva County ("the Geneva County property"). At the time 
the building was delivered, geocoordinates for the building were recorded 
on a delivery sheet. 
Evidence was presented that Tu rner had purchased the Geneva 
County property in 1991, that Turner had lived on the Geneva County 
property from 1991 to 1996, and that he did not live on the Geneva 
County property after 1996. After he moved from the Geneva County 
SC-2025-0453 
4 

property, Turner would visit th e land and would sometimes spend 
weekends there. In 2021, James Gough contacted Turner about 
purchasing the Geneva County property. Turner and Gough agreed that 
Gough would purchase the Geneva County property for $30,000. Gough 
wanted to save up the money to pay for the property, and Turner agreed. 
Turner also agreed that Gough coul d use the property and that he did 
not go down and visit the property after that time. However, he testified 
that Gough had told him that he had placed a gate on the property. He 
also agreed that, around the time the cabin was delivered, Gough had 
told him the cabin was on the property and that it might have been after 
the cabin had been delivered when Gough told him that. 
A call log for BHR was entered into evidence. The call log indicated 
that, on January 4, 2024, BHR received a telephone call. Notes from the 
call included a telephone number and stated, "property owner called and 
wanted to know if cust [sic] is paying bc [sic] the building is on his 
property. Told him I'd pass his info along to [Jack Horton]." Jack Horton, 
the repossession manager for BHR, te stified that he tried to call the 
telephone number provided, but no one answered. Horton entered a note 
stating, in pertinent part " WE NEED PROOF OF OWNERSHIP IF 
SC-2025-0453 
5 

PERSON CALLS BACK CLAIMING TO BE PROPERTY OWNER." 
(Bold typeface and capitalization in original.) 
Turner testified that, in 2024, Gough told him that he was ready to 
purchase the property; that, on Ma y 7, 2024, he went with Gough and 
Gough's wife to the office of Bruc e McLean, an attorney, to close the 
transaction; that he executed a de ed for the Geneva County property 
("the May 2024 deed"); that Gough paid him the $30,000; and that he 
delivered the May 2024 deed to Gough. Turner further testified that, at 
the time, he owed money on the Gene va County property to Troy Bank 
and Trust Company; that, after the cl osing, he and Gough went to Troy 
Bank and Trust; and that he paid off the loan at that time. The May 2024 
deed listed James Gough and his wife, Jennifer Gough, as the grantors. 
The May 2024 deed was never recorded in the probate court. 
On May 15, 2024, a contractor for BHR attempted to repossess the 
building. Geocoordinates were used to locate the building. However, the 
driver was not able to repossess th e building because there was a gate 
with a lock across the road. The dr iver was able to verify the serial 
number on the building. 
SC-2025-0453 
6 

Horton's notes from the call log indicated that the repossession 
driver telephoned him on May 15, 2024, and informed him that the 
building was "way off the road" and that there were locked gates. 
Horton's note further indicated: "Provided possible property owner's 
number from prior call. … He is going to see if he can get the recovery set 
up." Horton testified that, on May 16, 2024, he called the telephone 
number from the January 2024 telephone call. Horton's notes from that 
telephone call stated: 
"Called property owner at …. Mr. explained calling us 2 or 3 
times about the building being pi cked up. He added that we 
can either pay him to get it or make him a 'hell of a deal' on 
it. Explained we could rewrite the contract but he would be 
responsible for paying what is owed on the contract. I added 
that the account would first have to be paid current in order 
to do a rewrite and that would be over $1,400. I also informed 
Mr. that we do not pay to get our property back. Explained 
the process is he can allow driver to get the building or it will 
be turned over to the Legal dept and involve him and the 
customer. Mr. again mentioned trying to get the building off 
his property. Informed him he should have been told to 
provide proof of ownership and th en we could have tasked it 
for recovery. Mr. insisted that we owe him money. Told him 
I can see where he called us on ce (1/4/24) but he may have 
called the dealer and Mr. hung up. I never got his name. The 
number returns for James Christopher Gough. Notified Legal 
Dept." 

Horton testified that he changed the rating of the acco unt to "prelegal" 
which shifted the responsibility of the case to BHR's legal department. 
SC-2025-0453 
7 

 Jennifer Woods, the collection mana ger for BHR, testified that she 
was in charge of the prelegal depart ment and that, once an account was 
changed to prelegal, she would manage the status of that account going 
forward. Woods testified that she wa s not an attorney or a paralegal. 
The call log included an entry fr om May 17, 2024, which stated: 
"property located at coordinates …. is owned by James R. 
Turner." (Bold typeface in original.) It also included a mailing address 
in Enterprise. Woods testified that she made the determination that 
Turner was the owner of the Geneva County property and that that entry 
was made by her assistant. With regard to the process she used to 
determine that Turner was the owne r of the Geneva County property, 
Woods testified: 
" So we use a multitude of different formulas. The first thing 
we will do is we will bring up the delivery slip for the happy 
sheet, where we have the G.O. coordinates. And then we look 
at the delivery pictures. 

"And then at that point we bring up Google Earth and 
Bing Maps. And we compare the coordinates into Google 
Maps and Bing Maps to get the direct location. 

"And then once we determined that, we move over to 
something called BaseMaps. It's a hunting map. And it's for 
locating property owners, and we use it. 

SC-2025-0453 
8 

"We take that and formulate it into that address. And 
at that point, we still want to make sure that our delivery 
attempt and Google's and Bing's images are all still showing 
the same off BaseMaps. Because when you look at BaseMaps, 
you get a global image. On Ba seMaps it will calculate who 
the property owner is. At that point, we take that property 
owner. We write it down. 

"We go in to -- the next thing that we do, we run a 
TransUnion property search. So once we run the TransUnion 
property search, it matched. So then at that point, we use the 
Alabama GIS System. And through the process BaseMaps, 
TransUnion, and the Alabama GIS, it lists James Turner at 
… Enterprise, Alabama …, as the property owner." 

Woods agreed that the GIS System was "what the revenue commission 
downstairs, the tax collector, uses to list who owns the property." 
Subsequently, the following occurred: 
"[Turner's Counsel:] Would -- do you know what a title 
examination is? 

"[Woods:] I do not. 

"[Turner's Counsel:] Do you know what an owner's title 
insurance policy is? 

"[Woods:] I do not. 

"[Turner's Counsel:] Do yo u know what a title opinion 
is? 

"[Woods:] No. 

SC-2025-0453 
9 

"[Turner's Counsel:] Where yo u hire an attorney to do 
an examination of the records and to provide you with that 
information? 

"[Woods:] Okay. 

"[Turner's Counsel:] And you didn't do that in this case? 

"[Woods:] I did not." 

Woods testified that she gave Ph arming Capital's attorneys the 
information and documents they would n eed to file the complaint. She 
further testified that its attorneys di d not send the complaint to her for 
approval before the complaint was f iled and that its attorneys routinely 
filed complaints based on information she provided to them. 
 On May 17, 2024, Pharming Capital sued Turner in the trial court. 
The summons and complaint both incl uded only Turner's home address 
in Enterprise in Coffee County. The complaint alleged that Hedlund had 
executed the agreement for the building, that Hedlund had defaulted on 
the payments under the agreement, that, pursuant to the agreement, 
Pharming Capital was entitled to po ssession of the building, and that 
"the Defendant" had failed to relinquish possession of the building after 
a reasonable demand. It further alleged that "the Defendant is 
unlawfully detaining and possessing said Building contrary to the rights 
SC-2025-0453 
10 

of" Pharming Capital and that, "[u]pon information and belief, Defendant 
owns the property where the Building is located." The complaint did not 
state where the cabin was located and did not include any allegation that 
the building was located on property in Geneva County. The complaint 
requested, in pertinent part: 
"(a) That process issue according to law; and 

"(b) That Plaintiff have judgment against the 
Defendant or anyone holding over through or 
on the behalf of, or in conjunction with 
Defendant, or attempting to unlawfully 
prevent such repossession for possession of 
the above-described property;

leads.caseName: 111 Heitz Pl, Inc. v. Rodriguez
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
111 Heitz Pl, Inc. v Rodriguez 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06675 
 November 12, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 111 Heitz Pl, Inc., et al., appellants, 
 v 
 Vivian Rodriguez, defendant, Edward Elkins, respondent. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 12, 2026 
 2025-07095, (Index No. 602883/23) 
 Mark C. Dillon, J.P. 
 Paul Wooten 
 Laurence L. Love 
 Elena Goldberg Velazquez, JJ. 

 Idaye Braimah, Garden City, NY, for appellants. 
 Jeff Morgenstern, PLLC, Carle Place, NY, for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action, inter alia, to recover unpaid rent, the plaintiffs appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Maureen McHugh Heitner, J.), entered May 16, 2025. The order, insofar as appealed from, granted the motion of the defendant Edward Elkins for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him. 
 ORDERED that the order is reversed insofar as appealed from, on the law, with costs, and the motion of the defendant Edward Elkins for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him is denied. 
 In July 2020, the plaintiff Haribai Bhambhani, as landlord, entered into a lease agreement with the defendant Edward Elkins to lease certain premises in Hicksville to Elkins and, among others, the defendant Vivian Rodriguez as tenants. Elkins alleged that he vacated the premises in October 2021, leaving Rodriguez in sole possession. 
 In July 2022, the plaintiff 111 Heitz Pl, Inc. (hereinafter 111 Heitz), commenced a holdover proceeding in the District Court, Nassau County, against, among others, Elkins and Rodriguez, seeking possession of the premises and fair value of use and occupancy of the premises. It is undisputed that 111 Heitz did not serve Elkins in the holdover proceeding and proceeded only against Rodriguez. On October 17, 2022, the court entered a judgment of possession and a warrant of eviction against Rodriguez. Thereafter, Rodriguez and 111 Heitz entered into a so-ordered stipulation pursuant to which Rodriguez was permitted to remain in possession of the premises until February 24, 2023. 
 In February 2023, the plaintiffs commenced this action against Rodriguez and Elkins, inter alia, to recover unpaid rent accruing after October 1, 2021. Elkins moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him, arguing, among other things, that the action was barred by the doctrines of res judicata and collateral estoppel based on the judgment in the holdover proceeding, which did not award monetary damages. In an order entered May 16, 2025, the Supreme Court, inter alia, granted Elkins's motion. The plaintiffs appeal. 
 "The doctrine of res judicata operates to preclude the reconsideration of claims actually litigated and resolved in a prior proceeding, as well as claims for different relief against the [*2] same party which arise out of the same factual grouping or transaction, and which should have or could have been resolved in the prior proceeding" ( Jacobson Dev. Group, LLC v Grossman , 198 AD3d 956, 959 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see Paramount Pictures Corp. v Allianz Risk Transfer AG , 31 NY3d 64, 72 ; Gregg v Lan Zhen Chen , 220 AD3d 697 , 698). "Under New York's transactional approach to the rule, once a claim is brought to a final conclusion, all other claims arising out of the same transaction or series of transactions are barred, even if based upon different theories or if seeking a different remedy" ( Matter of Josey v Goord , 9 NY3d 386, 389-390 [internal quotation marks omitted]). "The doctrine of collateral estoppel, a narrower species of res judicata , precludes a party from relitigating in a subsequent action or proceeding an issue clearly raised in a prior action or proceeding and decided against that party or those in privity, whether or not the tribunals or causes of action are the same" ( Ryan v New York Tel. Co. , 62 NY2d 494, 500 ; see Babad v Oratz , 242 AD3d 807 , 808). "The doctrine of collateral estoppel applies when: (1) the issues in both proceedings are identical, (2) the issue in the prior proceeding was actually litigated and decided, (3) there was a full and fair opportunity to litigate in the prior proceeding, and (4) the issue previously litigated was necessary to support a valid and final judgment on the merits" ( Hossain v Hossain , 243 AD3d 894 , 895-896 [internal quotation marks omitted]). "The party seeking the benefit of collateral estoppel bears the burden of proving that the identical issue was necessarily decided in the prior action [or proceeding] and is decisive of the present action [or proceeding], and [t]he party against whom preclusion is sought bears the burden of demonstrating the absence of a full and fair opportunity to contest the prior determination" ( Matter of A. Ottavino Prop. Corp. v Incorporated Vil. of Westbury , 203 AD3d 920, 921 [internal quotation marks omitted]). 
 "[A] summary proceeding, being a possessory remedy, lies only against the tenant in possession and those in possession under the tenant" ( Park Prop. Dev. v Santos , 1 Misc 3d 16, 17 [App Term, 2d & 11th Jud Dists] [internal quotation marks omitted]; see LaCarrubba v Outdoors Clothing Corp. , 42 Misc 3d 136[A] , 2014 NY Slip Op 50119[U] [App Term, 9th & 10th Jud Dists]). According to Elkins's own submissions in support of his motion, he was no longer in possession of the premises when 111 Heitz commenced the holdover proceeding, and 111 Heitz did not proceed against him in the holdover proceeding. There was no determination on the merits of the plaintiffs' claims for rent arrears as against Elkins in the holdover proceeding, and therefore, the doctrines of res judicata and collateral estoppel do not apply ( see 1155 Nobo Assoc., LLC v New York Hosp. Med. Ctr. of Queens , 181 AD3d 937 , 938). Accordingly, the Supreme Court improperly concluded that the complaint was barred by the doctrines of res judicata and collateral estoppel, and should have denied Elkins's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him. 
 DILLON, J.P., WOOTEN, LOVE and GOLDBERG VELAZQUEZ, JJ., concur. 
 ENTER: 
 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

leads.caseName: Crosby Gibraltar, LLC v. Arora
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Crosby Gibraltar, LLC v Arora 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06686 
 November 12, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Crosby Gibraltar, LLC, respondent, 
 v 
 Ganesh Arora, et al., appellants, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 12, 2026 
 2024-05890, (Index No. 726628/22) 
 Betsy Barros, J.P. 
 Cheryl E. Chambers 
 Janice A. Taylor 
 Elena Goldberg Velazquez, JJ. 

 Biolsi Law Group, P.C., New York, NY (Steven Alexander Biolsi of counsel), for appellants. 
 Hasbani & Light, P.C., New York, NY (Danielle P. Light of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the defendants Ganesh Arora and Sureeyah Vitjathorn appeal from an order and judgment of foreclosure and sale (one paper) of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Tracy Catapano-Fox, J.), entered August 7, 2024. The order and judgment of foreclosure and sale, upon an order of the same court entered February 29, 2024, inter alia, granting those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendants Ganesh Arora and Sureeyah Vitjathorn, striking those defendants' answers, and for an order of reference, granted the plaintiff's unopposed motion to confirm a referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale, confirmed the referee's report, and directed the sale of the subject property. 
 ORDERED that the appeal is dismissed, except insofar as it brings up for review the order entered February 29, 2024 ( see CPLR 5511); and it is further, 
 ORDERED that the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale is affirmed insofar as reviewed; and it is further, 
 ORDERED that one bill of costs is awarded to the plaintiff. 
 The plaintiff commenced this action against, among others, the defendants Ganesh Arora and Sureeyah Vitjathorn (hereinafter together the defendants) to foreclose a mortgage on certain residential property located in Queens. The plaintiff moved, inter alia, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendants, to strike the defendants' answers, and for an order of reference. In an order entered February 29, 2024, the Supreme Court, among other things, granted those branches of the plaintiff's motion. In an order and judgment of foreclosure and sale entered August 7, 2024, the court granted the plaintiff's unopposed motion to confirm a referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale, confirmed the referee's report, and directed the sale of the property. The defendants appeal. 
 RPAPL 1304(1) requires that "at least ninety days before a lender, an assignee or a mortgage loan servicer commences legal action against the borrower, . . . including mortgage foreclosure, such lender, assignee or mortgage loan servicer shall give notice to the borrower" ( see [*2] Citibank, N.A. v Conti-Scheurer , 172 AD3d 17 , 20). "Strict compliance with RPAPL 1304 notice to the borrower or borrowers is a condition precedent to the commencement of a foreclosure action" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Adams , 202 AD3d 867, 868 [internal quotation marks omitted]). 
 A party can establish that a notice was sent through evidence of actual mailing ( see CIT Bank N.A. v Schiffman , 36 NY3d 550 , 556; U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Chiramannil , 205 AD3d 966, 968 ). Here, in opposition to the plaintiff's prima facie showing that it complied with RPAPL 1304, the defendants failed to raise a triable issue of fact ( see U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Chiramannil , 205 AD3d at 968 ; HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Espinal , 137 AD3d 1079, 1080 ). Contrary to the defendants' contention, with respect to the RPAPL 1304 notice sent to the defendants, the plaintiff was not required to include proof of its attorneys' authority to act on its behalf ( cf. Ocwen Loan Servicing LLC v Siame , 185 AD3d 408, 409 ; Flagstar Bank, FSB v Mendoza , 139 AD3d 898, 900 ). 
 "Compliance with RPAPL 1306 is a condition precedent to the commencement of a foreclosure action" ( Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Peralta , 239 AD3d 932 , 932 [internal quotation marks omitted]). "A proof of filing statement from the New York State Department of Financial Services is sufficient to establish, prima facie, that the plaintiff complied with RPAPL 1306" ( U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Chiramannil , 205 AD3d at 967 ). 
 Here, the plaintiff demonstrated, prima facie, its compliance with RPAPL 1306 by submitting a copy of a proof of filing statement from the New York State Department of Financial Services ( see U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Chiramannil , 205 AD3d at 968 ). In opposition, the defendants failed to raise a triable issue of fact. The defendants' contention that the plaintiff did not comply with the requirements of RPAPL 1306 because it omitted certain information from the filing is improperly raised for the first time on appeal ( see U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Solomon , 241 AD3d 749 , 750; Bank of Am., N.A. v Cudjoe , 157 AD3d 653 , 654). 
 The defendants' remaining contentions are without merit. 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendants, to strike the defendants' answers, and for an order of reference. 
 BARROS, J.P., CHAMBERS, TAYLOR and GOLDBERG VELAZQUEZ, JJ., concur. 
 ENTER: 
 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

 Laurence L. Love 
 James P. McCormack, JJ. 

 Justin F. Pane, P.C., Bohemia, NY (Daniel G. Eugene and Justin F. Pane of counsel), for appellant. 
 Robertson Anschutz Schneid Crane & Partners, PLLC, Westbury, NY (Joseph F. Battista of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the defendant Sofia Routier appeals from (1) an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (S. Betsy Heckman Torres, J.), dated November 21, 2022, and (2) an order and judgment of foreclosure and sale (one paper) of the same court entered November 28, 2022. The order granted the plaintiff's motion to confirm a referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale, and denied that defendant's cross-motion for leave to renew her opposition to those branches of the plaintiff's prior motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against that defendant, to strike that defendant's answer, and for an order of reference, which had been granted in an order of the same court (C. Randall Hinrichs, J.) dated June 24, 2019, and, upon renewal, for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against her. The order and judgment of foreclosure and sale, upon the order dated November 21, 2022, inter alia, confirmed the referee's report and directed the sale of the subject property. 
 ORDERED that the appeal from the order dated November 21, 2022, is dismissed; and it is further, 
 ORDERED that the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale is reversed, on the law, the plaintiff's motion to confirm the referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale is denied, that branch of the cross-motion of the defendant Sofia Routier which was for leave to renew her opposition those branches of the plaintiff's prior motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against that defendant, to strike that defendant's answer, and for an order of reference is granted, upon renewal, so much of the order dated June 24, 2019, as granted those branches of the plaintiff's prior motion is vacated, and thereupon those branches of the plaintiff's prior motion are denied, and the order dated November 21, 2022, is modified accordingly; and it is further, 
 ORDERED that one bill of costs is awarded to the defendant Sofia Routier. 
 The appeal from the order dated November 21, 2022, must be dismissed because the right of direct appeal therefrom terminated with the entry of the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale in the action ( see Matter of Aho , 39 NY2d 241, 248 ). The issues raised on the appeal from [*2] that order are brought up for review and have been considered on the appeal from the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale ( see CPLR 5501[a][1]). 
 On October 30, 2006, the defendant Sofia Routier (hereinafter the defendant) executed a note in the amount of $324,000 in favor of Homecomings Financial, LLC (hereinafter Homecomings). The note was secured by a mortgage on certain real property located in Suffolk County. 
 On January 26, 2017, the plaintiff, Homecomings's successor in interest, commenced this action to foreclose the mortgage against, among others, the defendant. The defendant's answer did not allege that the plaintiff failed to comply with RPAPL 1304. On February 12, 2018, the plaintiff moved, inter alia, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant, to strike the defendant's answer, and for an order of reference. In support of its motion, the plaintiff offered, among other evidence, purported proof that notices pursuant to RPAPL 1304 were properly sent to the defendant, but the plaintiff contended that, in any event, it was not required to prove RPAPL 1304 compliance as part of its prima facie burden due to the defendant's failure to raise it as an affirmative defense. The defendant submitted opposition to the plaintiff's motion, in which the defendant did not raise a defense relating to RPAPL 1304. In an order dated June 24, 2019, the Supreme Court, among other things, granted those branches of the plaintiff's motion, without making an express finding regarding the plaintiff's compliance with RPAPL 1304. 
 In August 2019, the plaintiff moved to confirm the referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale. The defendant opposed the motion and cross-moved for leave to renew her opposition to those branches of the plaintiff's prior motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant, to strike the defendant's answer, and for an order of reference and, upon renewal, for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against her, on the ground that the plaintiff failed to comply with RPAPL 1304. In support of her cross-motion, the defendant submitted her own affidavit, in which she denied receiving any RPAPL 1304 notice "in a manner that strictly complies with the law." In an order dated November 21, 2022, the Supreme Court granted the plaintiff's motion and denied the defendant's cross-motion. In an order and judgment of foreclosure and sale entered November 28, 2022, the court, upon the order dated November 21, 2022, inter alia, confirmed the referee's report and directed the sale of the subject property. The defendant appeals. 
 Contrary to the plaintiff's contention, the defendant did not waive the issue of noncompliance with RPAPL 1304 by failing to raise it in opposition to the plaintiff's prior motion, among other things, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant ( see HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Stein , 241 AD3d 661 , 663; Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Davidson , 202 AD3d 880, 882 ). The issue of noncompliance with RPAPL 1304 may be raised at any time prior to the entry of a judgment of foreclosure and sale ( see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Bancic , 203 AD3d 1130, 1133 ; U.S. Bank N.A. v Krakoff , 199 AD3d 859, 862 ). 
 Turning to the merits, RPAPL 1304(1) provides that "at least ninety days before a lender, an assignee or a mortgage loan servicer commences legal action against the borrower, including mortgage foreclosure, such lender, assignee or mortgage loan servicer shall give notice to the borrower." Proper service of RPAPL 1304 notice on the borrower or borrowers is a condition precedent to the commencement of a residential mortage foreclosure action ( see Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Cato , 243 AD3d 731 , 732; U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Mohammed , 197 AD3d 1205, 1207 ). RPAPL 1304 requires that the notice be sent by registered or certified mail, and also by first-class mail, to the last known address of the borrower ( see id. § 1304[2]). The plaintiff can establish strict compliance with RPAPL 1304 by submitting domestic return receipts, proof of a standard office procedure designed to ensure that items are properly addressed and mailed, or an affidavit from someone with personal knowledge that the mailing of the RPAPL 1304 notice actually happened ( see Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Cato , 243 AD3d at 733; Citibank, N.A. v Conti-Scheurer , 172 AD3d 17 , 21). Here, the affidavit of Vanessa Giorgiani, a vice president of the plaintiff's loan servicer, was insufficient to establish that the required notices were actually mailed, since she did not aver that she had personal knowledge of the mailing, did not describe any standard office procedure designed to ensure that the notices are mailed, and did not attach domestic return receipts for the mailing ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Thomas , 211 AD3d 1078, 1080 ; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Ezeji , 194 AD3d 909 ). Moreover, contrary to the plaintiff's contention, the plaintiff failed to submit any evidence to [*3] establish that the RPAPL 1304 requirement was inapplicable to the instant loan ( see Bank of Am., N.A. v Reed , 239 AD3d 800 , 804; JP Morgan Chase v Twersky , 202 AD3d 769, 771 ). Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have denied the plaintiff's motion to confirm the referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale, granted that branch of the defendant's cross-motion which was for leave to renew, and, upon renewal, denied those branches of the plaintiff's prior motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against her, to strike her answer, and for an order of reference. 
 Contrary to the defendant's contention, however, the Supreme Court properly denied that branch of the defendant's cross-motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against her on the ground that the plaintiff failed to comply with RPAPL 1304. A mere denial of receipt of an RPAPL 1304 notice is insufficient to establish entitlement to summary judgment dismissing the complaint ( see Citibank, N.A. v Conti-Scheurer , 172 AD3d at 20-21; see also Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Mangi , 222 AD3d 942, 945 ; U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Sadique , 178 AD3d 984 ). 
 The parties' remaining contentions are without merit. 
 BARROS, J.P., CHAMBERS, LOVE and MCCORMACK, JJ., concur.

 Darrell M. Joseph

leads.court: Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
leads.text:
United States Court of Appeals 
for the Fifth Circuit 
____________ 

No. 25-60618 
Summary Calendar 
____________ 

First Service Bank, 

Plaintiff—Appellee, 

versus 

Thomas L. Swarek, 

Defendant—Appellant. 
______________________________ 

Appeal from the United States District Court 
for the Southern District of Mississippi 
USDC No. 1:24-CV-20 
______________________________ 

Before Higginbotham, Smith, and Ho, Circuit Judges. 
Per Curiam:
* 
Thomas Swarek, proceeding pro se, appeals the district court’s grant 
of summary judgment in favor of First Service Bank (“FSB”) on his guaranty 
of a $50 million loan, as well as its alternative denial of his motion to set aside 
default and entry of default judgment. He challenges FSB’s authority to 
recover the full debt, the calculation of the judgment, and the district court’s 
_____________________ 
* This opinion is not designated for publication. See 5th Cir. R. 47.5. 
United States Court of Appeals 
Fifth Circuit 
FILED 
November 12, 2026 

Thomas B. Plunkett, III 
Clerk 
Case: 25-60618 Document: 103-1 Page: 1 Date Filed: 11/12/2026
No. 25-60618 
2 
reliance on evidence submitted with FSB’s summary judgment reply. He also 
contends that the default rulings rest on the same flawed merits analysis. We 
AFFIRM. 
I. 
In 2020, FSB entered into a $50,000,000 loan agreement with El 
Dorado Gas & Oil, Inc ., with Swarek as a guarantor. FSB subsequently sold 
a 95% participation interest in the loan to M S Facilities 2020 LLC ( “MS 
Facilities”), retaining a 5% interest and serving as the loan’s servicing agent. 
After the borrower defaulted, FSB accelerated the debt and sought to recover 
the outstanding balance from Swarek pursuant to his guaranty. 
FSB filed the present suit in January 2024, seeking judgment against 
Swarek for failure of his payment obligations . After Swarek did not timely 
answer, the clerk entered default, which Swarek promptly moved to set aside. 
FSB subsequently moved for summary judgment. Swarek opposed the 
motion, arguing that FSB could recover only its 5% interest in the loan and 
that MS Facilities was a necessary party. FSB responded with additional 
evidence concerning its authority to enforce the entire debt. The district 
court granted summar y judgment for FSB, concluding that it was 
contractually authorized to recover the full outstanding balance and that MS 
Facilities was not a required party. In the alternative, the court also denied 
Swarek’s motion to set aside default and granted FSB’s motion for default 
judgment. The court entered judgment for $54,928,751.83, which became 
final following dismissal of the remaining claims against another defendant. 
Swarek appealed. 
II. 
We review a district court’ s grant of summary judgment de novo, 
viewing all evidence in the light most favorable to the non -moving party and 
drawing all reasonable inferences in that party ’s favor. Dediol v. Best 
Case: 25-60618 Document: 103-1 Page: 2 Date Filed: 11/12/2026
No. 25-60618 
3 
Chevrolet, 655 F.3d 435, 439 (5th Cir. 2011). Summary judgment is proper 
when “the movant shows that there is no genuine dispute as to any material 
fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” Fed. R. 
Civ. P. 56(a). A genuine dispute of material fact exists “if the evidence is 
such that a reasonable jury could return a verdict for the non-moving party.” 
Crawford v. Formosa Plastics Corp., 234 F.3d 899, 902 (5th Cir. 2000) (quoting 
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242, 248 (1986)). 
III. 
The district court did not err in granting summary judgment. “[S]uits 
on promissory notes provide fit grist for the summary judgment mill.” 
Resolution Trust Corp. v. Starkey, 41 F.3d 1018, 1023 (5th Cir. 1995) (quoting 
FDIC v. Cardinal Oil Well Servicing Co., 837 F.2d 1369, 1371 (5th Cir. 1988)). 
FSB produced the loan documents, Swarek’s guaranty, and sworn evidence 
establishing default and the outstanding balance . Swarek does not dispute 
that he was late on payments owed to FSB. He instead contends that FSB 
lacked authority to recover the entire debt. Although FSB sold a 95% 
participation interest to MS Facilities, the participation and servicing 
agreements establish ed that FSB retained title to the loan and authority to 
enforce the entire obligation. And MS Facilities “support[ed] FSB’s decision 
to pursue this litigation for the full amount to the debt.” Swarek identifies no 
evidence creating a genuine dispute concerning FSB’s enforcement 
authority. Nor, as explained by the district court, was MS Facilities a required 
party to the action under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 19(a). 
Swarek also challenges the amount of the judgment, arguing that FSB 
failed to adequately substantiate its calculation of principal, interest, and fees. 
But Swarek did not raise these objections before the district court, instead 
challenging FSB’s authority to recover payment in full. He has therefore 
forfeited the argument on appeal. See Rollins v. Home Depot USA, 8 F.4th 393, 
Case: 25-60618 Document: 103-1 Page: 3 Date Filed: 11/12/2026
No. 25-60618 
4 
397–98. In any event, FSB submitted a sworn declaration itemizing the 
outstanding balance, and the loan agreement expressly authorized 
capitalization of deferred interest. Swarek has identified no evidence of an 
incorrect calculation to create a genuine dispute of material fact. 
Finally, Swarek challenges the district court’s reliance on evidence 
first submitted with FSB’s summary -judgment reply. We review such 
evidentiary rulings for abuse of discretion. Huynh v. Walmart Inc., 30 F.4th 
448,458 (5th Cir. 2022) (citation omitted). “[W]hen a party raises new 
arguments or evidence for the first time in a reply, the district court must 
either give the other party an opportunity to respond or decline to rely on the 
new arguments and evidence.” Ga. Firefighters ’ Pension Fund v. Anadarko 
Petroleum Corp., 99 F.4th 770, 774 (5th Cir. 2024) (citation omitted). Swarek 
was not denied the opportunity to respond. He neither objected to the 
evidence nor sought leave to file a surreply in the fifty -two days before the 
district court ruled. Nor has he demonstrated “ substantial prejudice ” 
warranting reversal. Huynh, 30 F.4th at 458. Therefore, there is no basis to 
find an abuse of discretion. 
As summary judgment was proper, we need not address the district 
court’s alternative default-judgment rulings. 
AFFIRMED.

leads.caseName: Hassan v. Askar Flash, L.L.C.
leads.text:
[Cite as Hassan v. Askar Flash, L.L.C., 2026-Ohio-4486.] 
 
COURT OF APPEALS OF OHIO 
 
EIGHTH APPELLATE DISTRICT 
COUNTY OF CUYAHOGA 
 
 
YAHIA HASSAN,   : 
   
 Plaintiff-Appellee, : 
                       No. 116215 
 v. : 
    
ASKAR FLASH, LLC, ET AL., : 
     
 Defendants-Appellants. :   
         
JOURNAL ENTRY AND OPINION 
 
JUDGMENT:  AFFIRMED 
RELEASED AND JOURNALIZED:  November 12, 2026 
          
 
Civil Appeal from the Cleveland Municipal Court 
Housing Division 
Case No. 2025-CVG-018806  
          
Appearances: 
 
Shapero & Green LLC, Brian Green, and Ricky Cutlip, for 
appellee.  
 
Seeley, Savidge, Ebert & Gourash Co., L.P.A., 
Christopher M. Corrigan, and Matthew T. Waters , for 
appellants. 
 
 
MICHELLE J. SHEEHAN, A.J.: 
 
{¶ 1} Defendants-appellants Askar Flash, LLC (“Askar”) and Ashbury 
Food, LLC (“Ashbury”) (collectively referred to as “Appellants”) appeal from the trial 
   
 
court’s judgment entry finding in favor of plaintiff -appellee Yahia Hassan 
(“Hassan”) on his forcible entry -and-detainer action.  Specifically, Appellants 
challenge the trial court’s adoption of the magistrate’s decision, alleging that the 
evidence did not support the magistrate’s decision and that the trial court erred in 
adopting a “corrected” version of the magis trate’s decision without providing an 
explanation for doing so. 
{¶ 2} After a thorough review of the law and record, we note that Appellants 
failed to file objections to the magistrate’s decision as set forth in Civ.R. 53(D)(3)(b).  
As such, they have forfeited all but plain error on their arguments concerning the 
magistrate’s findings on appeal.  Since Appellants fail to argue plain error with 
respect to the magistrate’s findings, we decline to address plain error and overrule 
the assignments of error challenging the magistrate’s findings.  With respect to 
Appellants’ challenge to the trial court’s adoption of the “corrected” magistrate’s 
decision, we find that the trial court was not required to provide an explanation 
when it approved the “corrected magistrate’s decision” and, therefore, did not abuse 
its discretion in failing to do so.   
{¶ 3} For these reasons, we overrule Appellants’ assignments of error and 
affirm the judgment of the trial court. 
I.  Background Overview 
A. Complaint 
{¶ 4} On December 16, 202 5, Hassan filed a complaint for forcible entry 
and detainer in Cleveland Municipal Court against Askar and Ashbury.  The 
   
 
complaint alleged that Hassan is the owner of the property located at 11025 Ashbury 
Ave., Cleveland, OH (the “premises”).  Askar and Ashbury are Ohio limited liability 
companies registered in the State of Ohio, which have their respective principal 
place of business located at the premises.   
{¶ 5} On April 12, 2025, Hassan and Askar entered into a commercial lease 
agreement for the premises.  The lease was subsequently assigned to Ashbury, which 
operates a convenience store at the premises. 
{¶ 6} On November 25, 2025, the complaint notes that Hassan served 
Appellants with a “3-day Notice to Vacate Premises,” which at the time of the filing 
of the complaint, the Appellants had not yet complied.  The complaint requested an 
order from the trial court concerning “[a] writ of restitution of the premises” and 
“[a]n award of all reasonable attorney fees and court c osts associated with this 
action.” 
B.  Answer and Counterclaims 
{¶ 7} On January 5, 2026, Appellants filed an answer and counterclaim to 
the complaint.  Appellants denied the allegations set forth in the complaint and 
claimed that (1) the complaint failed “to state a claim on which relief can be granted,” 
(2)  “[Hassan] failed to provide [Appellants] with any Notice of Default relative to 
any alleged violations of the lease as is expressly required by the terms and 
conditions of the lease[,]” (3) Hassan failed to provide Appellants an opportunity to 
cure the alleged violations, and (4) even if Appellants had violated the conditions set 
forth in the lease, the violations had been cured prior to the filing of the complaint.   
   
 
{¶ 8} The answer also raised several counterclaims against Hassan alleging 
vandalism and tortious interference.   
C.  Hearing 
{¶ 9} On January 13, 2026 , an eviction hearing was held before the 
magistrate.  Prior to the presentation of evidence, Hassan’s attorney noted that the 
hearing would be limited to the issue of illegal activity occurring on the premises in 
violation of the lease agreement. 
{¶ 10} Hassan testified that he is the owner of the premises where Appellants 
operate their business pursuant to the lease.  Hassan stated that the business has a 
C-1 alcohol license issued by the State of Ohio that only permits the sale of beer on 
the premises.  He stated that the license is currently issued under his wife’s name 
but was currently in the process of being transferred and that any violations of the 
license could cause an issue with the pending transfer. 
{¶ 11} Hassan testified that on November 5, 2025 , he observed vodka and 
wine products “for sale in the cooler.”  He also saw bottles of Fireball and High 
Noons in the coolers.  He explained that these products were not supposed to be sold 
at the premises “because they carry a high volume of alcohol or wine product in 
them.”  He proceeded to take photographs of these products.  Photographs of the 
display coolers containing these products were introduced at the hearing.  
{¶ 12} Hassan stated that he spoke to Muhammad Askar (“Muhammad”) 
and notified him that the sale of these products was illegal and that it could 
   
 
jeopardize the alcohol license.  H assan also advised them that his wife could be 
implicated since the license had not yet been transferred out of her name.   
{¶ 13} Hassan testified that even after notifying Appellants of this situation, 
the products remained at the premises.  Hassan stated that when he returned to the 
premises the following week, on November 12, 2025, the products were still in the 
cooler but had bee n moved from the top shelf to the bottom shelf of the cooler.  
When he returned a few days later, on November 18, 2025, he observed that the 
products had been moved behind the counter. 
{¶ 14} Muhammad testified on behalf of the Appellants.  Muhammad stated 
that he was aware that there was wine in the sales cooler on November 5, 2025, but 
the product was eventually placed at the bottom of the cooler by November 7, 2025.  
He testified that it was  no longer on display but could still be seen in the cooler.  
Muhammad testified that on either November 18 or 19, 2025, he removed all of the 
products from the store. 
D. Judgment 
{¶ 15} On February 13, 2026 , a magistrate’s decision titled “corrected 
magistrate’s decision,” which was signed by the magistrate, was filed on the docket.1  
 
1 Appellants attached a copy of the initial magistrate’s decision, prior to the correction, to 
their merit brief , in which the magistrate  recommended “[j]udgment for Defendant on 
Plaintiff’s on its [sic] first cause of action.”  This decision was not filed on the docket nor 
was it adopted, approved, or journalized by the trial court.  It is therefore not a part of the 
record on appeal , and we may not consider it.  State v. Westley, 2020-Ohio-809, ¶ 21, 
fn. 1 (8th Dist.)  (recognizing that documents attached to a party’s merit brief cannot be 
considered “since those records were not part of the record on appeal”), citing State v. 
Jones, 1993 Ohio App. LEXIS 4659, *6-7 (8th Dist. Sept. 30, 1993). 
   
 
The decision was dated February 5, 2026, and recommended that judgment should 
be “for [Hassan] on [his] first cause of action.”  The decision also included the 
following notice: 
Attention: A party may not assign as error on appeal any magistrate’s 
finding of fact or conclusion of law unless the party timely and 
specifically objects to that finding or conclusion as required by 
Civ.R. 53(d)(3)(b).  All objections to the magistrate’s decision must be 
filed in writing within fourteen days of the journalization of this 
decision.  Objections must be filed even if the trial court has 
provisionally adopted the magistrate ’s decision before the fourteen 
days for filing objections has passed.  Objections must comply with the 
Ohio Rules of Civil Procedure, and the local rules of this court.  For 
further information, consult the above rules or seek legal counsel. 
 
{¶ 16} On February 13, 2026 , the trial court approved and confirmed the 
“corrected magistrate’s decision,” finding for Hassan on his first cause of action. 
{¶ 17} The record does not include any objections to the “corrected 
magistrate’s decision” by Appellants. 
D.  Appeal 
{¶ 18} Appellants appealed the trial court’s decision adopting the corrected 
magistrate’s decision, presenting the following assignments of error for our review: 
1.  The trial court erred in finding in favor of [Hassan] on the first cause 
of action because Hassan did not prove each element of his claim 
against [Appellants] by a preponderance of the evidence. 
 
2.  The lower court erred in finding for in favor of Hassan on the first 
cause of action because [Appellants] proved that they had cured any 
alleged violation in accordance with the terms of the Lease Agreement. 
 
3.  The lower court erred in finding in favor of Hassan on the first cause 
of action because Hassan did not produce any evidence that Askar 
[had] engaged in illegal activity on the Premises. 
 
   
 
4.  The lower court erred in ruling for Hassan on the first cause of action 
because that decision was against the manifest weight of the evidence. 
 
5.  The lower court erred by arbitrarily and without explanation issuing 
a Corrected Magistrate’s Decision in which the Magistrate, using the 
same findings of fact and conclusions of law set forth in the Magistrate’s 
Decision, totally reversed the recommendati on made in the 
Magistrate’s Decision. 
 
6.  The lower court erred in failing to conclude that Hassan did not 
prove that [Appellants] violated the Lease Agreement by a 
preponderance of the evidence because the evidence was equipoise. 
   
II. Law and Analysis 
A. First, Second, Third, Fourth, and Sixth Assignments of Error 
{¶ 19} In the first, second, third, fourth, and sixth assigned errors for review, 
Appellants challenge the factual and legal conclusions set forth in the “corrected 
magistrate’s decision ,” which was approved and confirmed by the trial court.  
However, Appellants failed to file objections to the “corrected magistrate’s decision” 
below and have therefore forfeited these challenges on appeal. 
{¶ 20} Civ.R. 53(D) governs proceedings in matters referred to magistrates.  
Civ.R. 53(D)(3)(b) “imposes an affirmative duty on parties to submit timely, specific, 
written objections to the trial court, identifying any error of fact or law in the 
magistrate's decision.”  Dhillon v. Dhillon, 2024-Ohio-3022, ¶ 16 (8th Dist.), citing 
Marrs v. Mickel, 2023-Ohio-4528, ¶ 12 (8th Dist.), citing Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v. 
Lundeen, 2020-Ohio-28, ¶ 11.  If a party fails to properly object to a magistrate’s 
decision in accordance with Civ.R. 53(D)(3)(b), “it generally forfeits the right to 
   
 
assign those issues on appeal.”  Id., citing Marrs at ¶ 12, citing U.S. Bank, N.A. v. 
Matthews, 2017-Ohio-4075, ¶ 14 (8th Dist.). 
{¶ 21} The trial court approved the corrected magistrate’s decision on the 
same day it was filed.  Civ.R. 53(D)(4)(e)(i) provides that a trial court may enter a 
judgment adopting a magistrate’s decision within the 14 days permitted for filing 
objections.  If a pa rty files a timely objection within those 14 days, the objections 
“shall operate as an automatic stay of execution of the judgment until the court 
disposes of those objections and vacates, modifies, or adheres to the judgment 
previously entered.”  Civ.R. 5 3(D)(4)(e)(i).  “Under this rule, the failure to file 
objections within the trai

leads.caseName: J & J Invests. of Ohio Inc. v. Hooper
leads.text:
[Cite as J & J Invests. of Ohio Inc. v. Hooper, 2026-Ohio-4480.] 
 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          
COURT OF APPEALS OF OHIO 
 
EIGHTH APPELLATE DISTRICT 
COUNTY OF CUYAHOGA 
 
J & J INVESTMENTS OF OHIO INC., : 
 
 Plaintiff-Appellee, : 
   No. 116062 
 v. : 
 
ANGELA HOOPER, : 
   
 Defendant-Appellant. : 
          
 
JOURNAL ENTRY AND OPINION 
 
  JUDGMENT:  REVERSED AND REMANDED 
RELEASED AND JOURNALIZED:  November 12, 2026 
          
 
Civil Appeal from the Cleveland Municipal Court 
Housing Division 
Case Nos. 2025-CVG-012141 and 2025-CVG-012811 
          
Appearances: 
 
Powers Friedman Linn, PLL, Kyle Ripma, and Rachel E. 
Cohen, for appellee. 
 
The Legal Aid Society of Cleveland, Joseph C. Tomino , 
and Barbara A. Reitzloff, for appellant. 
 
 
MICHAEL JOHN RYAN, J.: 
 
 Defendant-appellant Angela Hooper (“Hooper”) appeals from the 
trial court’s December 24, 2025 judgment entry granting plaintiff -appellee J&J 
Investments of Ohio Inc.’s (“J&J”) motion for partial summary judgment in its 
 
 
forcible-entry-and-detainer action.  For the following reasons, we reverse and 
remand. 
Factual and Procedural History 
 Hooper has been a residential tenant living in a home located on 
Kenneth Avenue in Cleveland (“the property”) for over ten years.  In September 
2023, J&J took over property management of the property on behalf of the property 
owner.  Beginning in October 2023, Hooper and J&J entered into a month -to-
month lease agreement.  Since J&J be gan managing the property, Hooper has 
reported various issues with the property to J&J.  These issues include severe water 
leaks and the resulting water damage, such as mold growth and lifting and damaging 
floor coverings.   
 On April 17, 2025, Hooper served J&J with a final request for repairs, 
pursuant to R.C. 5321.07, via email. 
 On May 19, 2025, J&J served Hooper with a notice of termination of 
her tenancy via email, informing Hooper that her tenancy would terminate on June 
30, 2025.  Hooper did not vacate the premises.  Instead, at some point following the 
notice of termination, Hooper submitted a complaint to the City of Cleveland ’s 
Department of Building and Housing and initiated a rent deposit.  
 The department of building and housing conducted an inspection of 
the property on June 30, 2025, and on July 16, 2025, it issued a violation notice to 
the property owner, identifying 17 violations of Cleveland’s housing code. 
 
 
 On July 18, 2025, J&J issued a three-day notice to Hooper to vacate 
the premises; the notice was affixed to the front door of the property.  Again, Hooper 
did not vacate the premises. 
 As a result, J&J filed two separate complaints in the Housing Division 
of the Cleveland Municipal Court.  First, on August 15, 2025, in 
Case No. 25CVG012141, J&J filed a complaint and application to release rent 
(“the rent release case”).  J&J alleged that Hooper had deposited a rent payment in 
the sum of $700 with the court, that Hooper failed to comply with the notice 
requirements set forth in R.C. 5321.07, and further, that J&J was not in violation of 
“any obligation imposed upon it by the rental agreement or any obligation imposed 
upon it by any building, housing, health or safety code.” 
 Second, on August 26, 2025, in Case No. 25CVG012811, J&J filed the 
within complaint for forcible entry and detainer against Hooper ( “the eviction 
case”).  J&J alleged that Hooper had unlawfully and forcibly detained J&J from 
possession of the property since July 24, 2025.  Hooper raised a retaliation defense 
under Cleveland Cod. Ord. (“CCO”) 375.08. 
 The trial court consolidated the two complaints.  
 Hooper and J&J filed cross -motions for partial summary judgment 
related to the eviction case.  Hooper attached correspondence between herself and 
J&J and photos corroborating her complaints to her motion for summary judgment.  
J&J attached an affidavit from James Penner (“Penner”), a property manager 
 
 
employed by J&J, along with a copy of the lease agreement between J&J and Hooper 
and additional correspondence. 
 On December 24, 2025, the trial court granted J&J’s motion for 
partial summary judgment, finding that there is a conflict between R.C. 5321.03 and 
CCO 375.08.  The court further found that R.C. 5321.02, et seq. , preempt CCO 
375.08’s protection from retaliatory terminations of tenancy and, therefore, J&J was 
entitled to evict Hooper.  The court simultaneously denied Hooper’s motion for 
partial summary judgment, holding that Hooper did not establish that there is no 
genuine iss ue of material fact as to whether the housing code violations at the 
property materially affected Hooper’s health and safety. 
 Hooper appeals, presenting five assignments of error for our review: 
I.  The trial court erred in holding that R.C. 5321.03 preempts 
CCO 375.08 because CCO 375.08’s prohibition on retaliatory 
terminations of tenancy is not in conflict with R.C. 5321.03’s license 
of eviction of holdover tenants even with retaliatory intent. 
II.  The trial court erred in holding that R.C. 5321.19 preempts 
CCO 375.08, because CCO 375.08 is part of the Housing Code of the 
City of Cleveland, and R.C. 5321.19 excludes Housing Codes from its 
alleged preemptions. 
III.  The trial court erred in holding that R.C. 5321.19 and R.C. 5321.20 
preempt CCO 375.08, because R.C. 5321.19 and R.C. 5321.20 are not 
in conflict with CCO 375.08. 
IV.  The trial court erred in holding that R.C. 5321.19 and R.C. 5321.20 
preempt CCO 375.08, because R.C. 5321.19 and R.C. 5321.20 are not 
general laws. 
V.  The trial court erred in not applying Hooper’s affirmative defense 
of retaliation under CCO 375.08 to its factual findings regarding 
Ms. Hooper’s complaints to J&J of its violations of R.C. 5321.04. 
 
 
Law and Analysis 
 Appellate review of a trial court ’s grant of summary judgment is 
de novo.  Grafton v. Ohio Edison Co., 77 Ohio St.3d 102, 105 (1996).   Pursuant to 
Civ.R. 56(C), summary judgment is appropriate when (1) there is no genuine issue 
of material fact, (2) the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law, and 
(3) reasonable minds can come to but one conclusion and that conclusion is adverse 
to the non moving party, said party being entitled to have the evidence construed 
most strongly in their favor.  Cleveland v. State, 2013-Ohio-1186,  ¶ 8 (8th Dist.), 
citing Horton v. Harwick Chem. Corp., 73 Ohio St.3d 679 (1995), paragraph three 
of the syllabus.  The party moving for summary judgment bears the burden of 
showing that there is no genuine issue of material fact and that it is entitled to 
judgment as a matter of law.  Id., citing Dresher v. Burt, 75 Ohio St.3d 280 (1996). 
 In her first assignment of error, Hooper contends that the trial court 
erred in finding that R.C. 5321.02 and 5321.03 preempt CCO 375.08.  We agree.   
 R.C. 5321.02 prohibits retaliatory action by a landlord.  The section  
provides in relevant part as follows: 
(A) Subject to section 5321.03 of the Revised Code, a landlord may not 
retaliate against a tenant by increasing the tenant’s rent, decreasing 
services that are due to the tenant, or bringing or threatening to bring 
an action for possession of the tenant’s premises because: 
(1) The tenant has complained to an appropriate governmental agency 
of a violation of a building, housing, health, or safety code that is 
applicable to the premises, and the violation materially affects health 
and safety; [or] 
 
 
(2) The tenant has complained to the landlord of any violation of 
section 5321.04 of the Revised Code[.] 
(Emphasis added.)  R.C. 5321.02(A).  
 R.C. 5321.03 governs actions by landlords and provides in relevant 
part: 
(A) Notwithstanding section 5321.02 of the Revised Code, a landlord 
may bring an action under Chapter 1923 of the Revised Code for 
possession of the premises if: 
. . . 
(4) The tenant is holding over the tenant’s term. 
 According to J&J, R.C. 5321.02 (A) and 5321.03 conflict with 
CCO 375.08, and because of Hooper’s holdover-tenant status, J&J properly initiated 
this eviction action against Hooper under the State’s statutes.   
 CCO 375.08 largely mirrors R.C. 5321.02(A), with one key exception. 
It provides: 
(a) subject to division (d) of this section, a landlord may not retaliate 
against a tenant by increasing the tenant’s rent, decreasing services 
that are due to the tenant, bringing or threatening to bring an action 
for possession of the tenant’s premises, terminating or threatening to 
terminate the tenant’s rental agreement, or refusing to renew the 
tenant’s rental agreement or to continue the tenant’s tenancy  
because: 
(1) The tenant has complained to an appropriate governmental agency 
of a violation of a building, housing, health, or safety code that is 
applicable to the premises, and the violation materially affects health 
and safety; 
(2) The tenant has complained to the landlord of any violation of 
R.C. 5321.04[.] 
(Emphasis added.)  CCO 375.08. 
 
 
 Thus, while both R.C. 5321.02(A) and CCO 375.08(a) provide that a 
landlord may not retaliate against a tenant by increasing rent, decreasing services, 
or bringing or threatening to bring an action for possession of the premises, 
CCO 375.08(a) goes a step further by adding protection for a tenant from a landlord 
terminating or threatening to terminate the rental agreement, or refusing to renew 
the rental agreement.  We find that the extra protection CCO 375.08 provides is a 
permissible exercise of the city’ s home rule authority  and does not conflict with 
R.C. 5321.02(A).   
 The Home Rule Amendment to the Ohio Constitution authorizes 
municipalities to exercise “all powers of local self -government and to adopt and 
enforce within their limits such local police, sanitary and other similar regulations, 
as are not in conflict with general laws.”  Ohio Const., art. XVIII § 3.  The intent of 
the Home Rule Amendment is “to empower municipalities to establish different 
forms of local self-government, to implement local ordinances not in conflict with 
general laws of the state and to ‘do those things . . . which are not forbidden by the 
lawmaking power of the state. ’”  (Citation omitted.)  Am. Fin. Servs. Assn. v. 
Cleveland, 2006-Ohio-6043, ¶ 26. 
 Courts use a three -part test to evaluate whether a municipality has 
exceeded its powers under the Home Rule Amendment: “A state statute takes 
precedence over a local ordinance when (1) the ordinance is an exercise of police 
power, rather than local self-government, (2) the statute is general law, and (3) the 
ordinance is in conflict with the statute.”  Mendenhall v. Akron, 2008-Ohio-270, 
 
 
¶ 17; see also Canton v. State, 2002-Ohio-2005, ¶ 9 (establishing the test utilized in 
Mendenhall). 
 Hooper concedes that CCO 375.08 is an exercise of police power but 
maintains that the State’s statutes do not preempt the city’s ordinance because they 
do not conflict with it an d because the State ’s statutes are not general laws.   
We agree. 
 Regarding whether there is a conflict, “[T]he test is whether the 
ordinance permits or licenses that which the statute forbids and pro

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF APPEALS OF WEST VIRGINIA 
 
September 2026 Term 
_____________ 
 
No. 23-728 
_____________ 
 
TIMBERLINE FOUR SEASONS UTILITIES, INC., AND  
CANAAN VALLEY PUBLIC SERVICE DISTRICT, 
Respondents Below, Petitioners, 
 
V. 
 
KAPITUS SERVICING, INC., 
Petitioner Below, Respondent. 
           
Appeal from the Intermediate Court of Appeals 
No. 23-ICA-22 
(Circuit Court of Tucker County, Civil Action No. CC-47-2022-C-4) 
 
REVERSED AND REMANDED 
           
 
Submitted: September 11, 2026 
Filed: November 12, 2026 
 
Martin P. Sheehan, Esq. 
Sheehan & Associates, PLLC 
Wheeling, West Virginia 
Attorney for Petitioner Timberline Four 
Seasons Utilities, Inc. 
 
John W. Cooper, Esq.  
Cooper & Preston, PLLC 
Davis, West Virginia

Ann Starcher, Esq.
